#3407. The iPhone Duo Is Getting Face Unlock

Apple dropped iOS 27.2.1 last week, patching a handful of security vulnerabilities and bugs—including two iMessage flaws that let people read messages they shouldn't. But while most of us are running this version (or should install it as soon as possible), others are running something different—iOS 27.3.

Apple is currently beta testing the third major update in the iOS 27 era, and anyone—developer and public tester alike—is free to install it at their leisure. With it, comes the return of the Health app, vertical Safari tabs, and Siri AI app actions, among other new features. But for users of Apple's first foldable, the iPhone Duo, iOS 27.3 brings two rather notable changes—both of which are for the better.

With the second iOS 27.3 developer beta, Apple is introducing face unlock for the iPhone Duo. The foldable famously ships with Touch ID, the first new iPhone since the third-gen iPhone SE to do so. While that isn't a problem per se, many of us are used to unlocking our iPhones with our faces. This update just lets new Duo owners keep up with that muscle memory.

Now, take note: This isn't Face ID. No software update can introduce new hardware, so the iPhone Duo still doesn't have the camera tech required to power Apple's Face ID system. As such, the Duo's face unlock is likely not as secure as Face ID on other iPhones. Perhaps that's why your iPhone Duo will require Touch ID for Apple Pay and passwords, or after 45 minutes of inactivity. This feature seems to be one of pure convenience: If you want to be able to unlock your Duo with your face (at least, some of the time), you can.

What's more, this isn't a default setting. If you're running the beta, or if you're reading this after iOS 27.3 drops, you can find the option in Settings > Touch ID & Passcode.

Apple made a big deal about the continuity involved with opening and closing the iPhone Duo. As you do, your content moves with you seamlessly—a very Apple thing to do. That said, you might expect folding the Duo to lock it, but it doesn't. You need to hit the side button to actually put the phone to sleep.

iOS 27.3 changes that. If you so choose, you can enable a setting to lock your Duo whenever you close it. That won't work for everyone, of course—some users may still want to move between modes without worrying about locking their Duos. But for those who would rather lock their devices whenever they fold them up, the new option is under Settings > Display & Brightness.

#3406. iPhone 18, iPhone Air 2 get new release timing updates

Apple only launched high-end ‘Pro’ and ‘Duo’ iPhones this fall, marking a departure from previous years when more affordable models debuted too. But iPhone 18 and iPhone Air 2 are still coming, and a new report offers an update on release timing.

A new report from Kim Yeong-ho at ETNews provides a fresh update on timing for the iPhone 18 and iPhone Air 2.

Rumors have indicated for well over a year that Apple planned to push these models out of the typical fall launch window and introduce them in early 2027 instead.

Per ETNews, Samsung and LG are providing the display panels for the new models, with Samsung the sole supplier for iPhone Air 2 and both companies splitting orders for iPhone 18. And their mass production plans signal a March release for the products.

Samsung Display plans to begin mass production in January, while LG Display will start late this year…The Korean panel makers appear to be aligning their production plans with an expected March launch.

A March launch window lines up well with when Apple tends to ramp up product introductions following a slower winter. Earlier this year, iPhone 17e debuted in March alongside new Macs and the iPad Air.

The year before, however, the iPhone 16e arrived in February instead.

With Apple shaking up its normal iPhone rollout schedule, it was anyone’s guess how soon the new models would debut. But a March launch makes sense and gives Apple a trio of new iPhones every six months—three unveiled in September, and another three in March.

#3405. Hogwarts Legacy 2 Official Release Update Issued By Warner Bros

Despite the controversy surrounding its launch, there is no denying that Hogwarts Legacy dominated the gaming sphere in 2023, with the Harry Potter-inspired RPG even going on to become the best-selling game of the year.

As such, it was not long before a sequel was announced, and over the past three years, Avalanche Software has been hard at work getting ready to send players back to Hogwarts School of Witchcraft and Wizardry.

It may have been the best-selling game of 2023, but Hogwarts Legacy did not come without its downfalls, especially as it did not receive any expansions or substantial post-game content drops. As such, fans are feeling mixed over a sequel. Will it expand on the open-world and offer long-term content, or will it be much of the same?

At the time of writing, Hogwarts Legacy 2 does not have a release date, or even a release window, despite previous rumors suggesting that it would coincide with the upcoming launch of the Harry Potter television show, which is set to debut on Christmas Day. However, it is unlikely that Hogwarts Legacy 2 is going to pop up over the next month, so we can safely assume that it will be 2027 at the earliest.

It was back in October that Warner Bros., the publishers behind Hogwarts Legacy, issued a statement on the game's progress, and after Paramount acquired Warner Bros. Discovery, it was confirmed that Warner Bros. Games would merge with Paramount Games Studio to create one giant gaming division.

It will be this gaming division that works on Hogwarts Legacy 2, but, as mentioned, no further information has been revealed, and fans are yet to see any gameplay or substantial updates. As such, its potential cancellation has been a subject of worry for fans, but according to a letter to shareholders discussing WB's games division, WB's strategy will be to focus on its most successful franchises, with Harry Potter being one of them. "We expect Games to more meaningfully contribute to segment profitability going forward as our pipeline expands," the statement reads, "including the second installment of Hogwarts Legacy."

With The Game Awards taking place on December 10, we can only hope that this next major gaming event will spare a moment for Hogwarts Legacy 2, and it would be perfect timing in the lead-up to the Harry Potter television show, especially as the two projects are rumored to be working together closely. However, this is mere speculation, and for now, we will have to wait with bated breath to see what comes next for the franchise.

Back in 2023, our very own William Cennamo awarded Hogwarts Legacy an almost perfect 9/10, with his review reading:

Hogwarts Legacy is a wonderful game filled to the brim with adventures to be had, activities to engage in, and secrets to be found. The school and the surrounding areas have been recreated beautifully, and players will easily lose hours lost in the whimsical splendor of this wizarding world.

#3404. Rian Johnson Leaves the Door Open to Star Wars Return: ‘It’s a World I Deeply Love’

Rian Johnson isn’t writing a Star Wars movie, but he isn’t ruling one out, either.

Responding to a question from IndieWire during an in-conversation event at the 23rd Marrakech International Film Festival, the writer/director of “Star Wars: The Last Jedi” was clear that his next project lies elsewhere: “I’m already writing the next thing I’m going to do, and it’s not a Star Wars thing, or in that genre,” he said.

“I’m very much enjoying just making my own stuff, but I mean, if the opportunity presented itself,” Johnson said, nodding. “It’s a world I deeply love. It’s also a group of people I love.”

“I love Star Wars more now than I ever have,” he added. “And it’s exciting to me that there are a lot of different voices now taking cracks at it.” The timing is hard to ignore. Related Stories Box Office: ‘Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping’ Debuts to Mighty $120 Million, Reviving Lionsgate’s Most Important Franchise Box Office: A24’s ‘You Can See Everything’ Crosses $100 Million Globally

Johnson’s remarks land just as Lucasfilm appears to be turning back toward the corner of the saga he helped shape. Polygon reported that two long-gestating features, “Star Wars: New Jedi Order” and an untitled film from Dave Filoni, are still listed as in development by Production Weekly, despite months of silence and the soft box office performance of “The Mandalorian & Grogu.”

“New Jedi Order” would theoretically bring back actress Daisy Ridley as Rey roughly 15 years after “The Rise of Skywalker,” rebuilding the Jedi Order that “The Last Jedi” so memorably called into question. Sharmeen Obaid-Chinoy is attached to direct, with George Nolfi now writing after earlier drafts from Damon Lindelof and Justin Britt-Gibson, and a stint by Bond 26 screenwriter Steven Knight. The film was pulled from its December 17, 2027 release date in May 2025. Meanwhile, “Star Wars: Starfighter,” the Shawn Levy-directed film starring Ryan Gosling and set five years after “The Rise of Skywalker,” remains the only Star Wars feature with a firm date: May 28, 2027.

In 2017, the year “The Last Jedi” hit theaters, Lucasfilm announced that Johnson would create a new Star Wars trilogy. Those films have yet to materialize, but Johnson had warm words for Filoni, who took on the role of Lucasfilm’s president and chief creative officer in January: “Dave Filoni I got to know while making ‘The Last Jedi’, and he’s a wonderful guy who really has the spirit of Star Wars in him,” he said. “All the Lucasfilm folks are awesome.”

Later, answering questions from the audience, Johnson described “The Last Jedi” as “the most joyful process of any movie I’ve ever made”, despite the challenge of stepping from his own original films into what he called a contested mythology.

“I’m a huge, huge fan of George Lucas, and I’ve read a lot about when he was writing the original Star Wars, how personal it was for him,” Johnson continued. “I think especially with something that has a deep cultural impact, and that belongs to everybody, that makes it even more important… to make sure it’s coming from a personal perspective and something that’s deeply on fire inside you, as opposed to thinking, ‘what’s gonna please this person and this person and this person’. That leads to homogeneity, to repeating yourself and to something that feels dead on screen.”

As a middle chapter, “The Last Jedi” drew directly on Johnson’s childhood experience of “The Empire Strikes Back,” though not as something to copy. “I didn’t want to imitate ‘The Empire Strikes Back’,” Johnson said. “What I wanted to get to was the heart of what that movie has, which is this center part of life where your job is to fail, and your job is to learn from that and to get up and keep moving forward.”

He drew a distinction between a film having a moral compass and having a moral. The compass, he said, “comes from the entire mass of every single creative decision made by the writer, or director, or whole team.”

Johnson also reflected on the only two composers he has worked with. His cousin Nathan Johnson has scored his films since the pair started making movies together at age ten: “Nathan is the first person to read the script; he’s on set for the entire shoot so it’s very much a collaboration.”

John Williams, he said, is also “a miracle of a human being”, and working with him was the opposite experience. “You give him the movie and then the first time I hear any music is when we’re on the scoring stage, and there are 200 musicians playing it.”

If Johnson does return to Star Wars, it seems he won’t be thinking about franchise strategy. “For me it’s not about thinking about IP, it’s about stories,” he said. “I deeply believe the only way to actually make a movie that matters and is worth something is to have your eyes nowhere else except on making that movie. What is the story we’re telling? Why are we telling it? Why do we care about it?”

“Outside of that bubble,” Johnson added, “I’ll leave it to the executives.”

With those executives now steering Star Wars back toward Rey and the post-“Rise of Skywalker” era, the bubble may be closer to his than it has been in years.

#3403. iPhone Duo is getting three new features in iOS 27.3

iOS 27.3 launches next month and includes several exciting changes for iPhone Duo, here’s what’s new for Apple’s foldable model.

Apple is granting iPhone Duo users one of their biggest feature requests: face unlock is coming with iOS 27.3.

Face unlock isn’t a full-fledged Face ID, and it doesn’t work for features like Apple Pay, but it is a convenient new option for unlocking your iPhone Duo just by looking at it. Per Apple:

Use the front camera, along with a recent Touch ID or passcode authentication, to quickly unlock iPhone Duo when it’s closed. Face recognition data never leaves your device.

If your iPhone Duo has gone unused for 45 minutes or more, face unlock won’t work and you’ll need to authenticate with Touch ID or your passcode. But for most users, that probably just means using Touch ID first thing in the morning, then relying on face unlock the rest of the day.

On a related note, you can also enable Attention Aware features in iOS 27.3. These are available whether you use the face unlock feature or not, but are limited to the outer display. Once enabled, they can automatically lower the volume of alarms and timers, keep the display from dimming, and more.

Read more: iOS 27.3 adds new face unlock feature for iPhone Duo

Reachability is available on other iPhone models to move onscreen content down vertically, closer to your thumb. But on iPhone Duo with iOS 27.3, Apple has a unique twist on the feature.

Instead of helping you reach content vertically, Reachability on iPhone Duo works horizontally.

If you’re using the outer screen and find that buttons or other UI elements are out of reach, you can swipe from the side to have onscreen content shift closer to your thumb.

You can always disable Reachability if you find yourself accidentally triggering it too often. But if one-handed iPhone Duo use gives you trouble, Reachability is a great new option to have.

Read more: iOS 27.3 introduces new iPhone Duo feature for one-handed use

What should happen when you close your iPhone Duo’s folding screen? Apple has found that users have different preferences. Some want the iPhone to stay unlocked for continued use, while others prefer that it automatically locks when closed.

In iOS 27.3, Apple adds a new setting so users can enable whichever behavior they prefer.

By default, iPhone Duo will work as it always has, staying unlocked after being closed. But inside Settings ⇾ Display & Brightness, iOS 27.3 provides the option of automatically locking upon being closed instead. You could achieve something similar before with Shortcuts, but now there’s a built-in setting too.

It’s not exactly a “new feature,” but iPhone Duo users will also find that the system keyboard has changed in iOS 27.3. Apple tweaked the outer display keyboard to push keys closer together and make one-handed use easier.

Here’s a comparison of the old and new keyboards via Beta Profiles on X:

iOS 27.3 beta tweaks iPhone Duo's outer display keyboard, with narrower keys and a slightly thinner, smaller font. pic.twitter.com/BDKCBZc52Z

Read more: iOS 27.3 changes the iPhone Duo keyboard, here’s how

#3402. Forget Taylor Sheridan, This is the Master of the Modern Western

Westerns have continuously trickled down in numbers as a genre for film and TV through the decades. While neo-Westerns seem to get a lot of traction, with a filmmaker like Taylor Sheridan having a filmography filled almost completely with entries in the genre—including his epic American Frontier Trilogy—there are few traditional Westerns that still get released to a wide audience. An argument could be made that there isn't much of a market anymore, or maybe that a lot of people just don't like Westerns, but that's about as much a blanket statement as saying you don't like action movies or chick flicks. That's fine if you don't like Nicholas Sparks knockoffs, but if you besmirch The Princess Bride or When Harry Met Sally by lumping them in with that sort, you best prepare to have a donnybrook on your hands. Rather, when it comes to traditional Westerns, short of homages or parodies, very few directors seem to have a deep desire to make them. That is, of course, except for the man with no first name given, and that's S. Craig Zahler.

The character actor of directors, S. Craig Zahler continues to work under the radar of general audiences, even though the movies he's made have been widely well-received by critics. He's a writer/director with a succinct style—bordering on niche—that's recognizable for its lockdown visual style, methodical pace, and engrossing, stage play-like dialogue, contrasting against viciously brutal violence and inhuman villains. All of this was established with his debut film, Bone Tomahawk, which is about a group of cowboys in the Old West, led by Sheriff Hunt (Kurt Russell), working to save the town doctor, Mrs. O'Dwyer (Lili Simmons), from savage, cannibalistic troglodytes. To put it into context, if you've ever heard the Mark Twain quote where he compared masterful writing to wine, and his to water...well, Zahler's movies are like the film-making equivalent of a White Monster Energy Drink (i.e. not for everybody, but the ones who like them will REALLY like them).

Aside from Bone Tomahawk, Zahler has also quietly flexed his Western skills by both being the uncredited screenwriter of last year's underrated Frontier Crucible, and by being a prolific novelist, with his two most famous being A Congregation of Jackals and Wraiths of the Broken Land, which, combined with Bone Tomahawk, are thematically linked to make a twisted Western trilogy. Wraiths of the Broken Land will also forever live as a "What could have been" scenario since it was announced back in 2016 to be adapted by Ridley Scott and Drew Goddard, but has since languished in the fires of Development Hell. Presumably because of how dark the novel gets and Zahler's distinct style being hard to sell to general audiences.

If spaghetti Westerns were considered subversions of traditional Westerns, Zahler's stories are subversions of spaghetti Westerns. Zahler's biggest strength as a storyteller is his ability to craft his stories into twists and turns that you're not expecting, and to go hard with wherever the story leads him. His method is to write each day until he shocks himself with what comes out, working from the idea that if he surprises himself while writing, the audience won't see it coming, either. That's probably how he came up with the horrid things that can be done with fishhooks, dead baby turtles, rifle barrels heated over an open fire, and everything about the "Wishbone" scene in Bone Tomahawk.

There's a blunt harshness to his action and violence, and especially the depiction of life on the frontier. He doesn't play favorites, and isn't afraid to shock and abhor his viewers or readers under the guise of telling the stories the way he wants to tell them. Sometimes, that means the lead characters are just as cruel as the villains, and almost without fail, that means the villains are pitiless and verge on being inhuman entities. It's like Zahler read Blood Meridian before writing A Congregation of Jackals and thought Judge Holden was too affable and normal looking, so he came up with Quinlan and his gang. And then he put Blood Meridian down because Cormac McCarthy's lack of quotations and speech tags around dialogue can be hard to follow sometimes . . .I'm guessing.

It's a different kind of Man With No Name.

What makes Zahler's stories so good is that even though their content might be too disturbing for some, his characters are consistently very fleshed-out and captivating to follow. And for every morally gray character, there are a few, like Sheriff Hunt in Bone Tomahawk and Merrick Beckford (Myles Clohessy) in Frontier Crucible, who feel like they could've come right out of a John Ford Western just for how noble they are. And in some cases, what actually makes the more disturbing things even more upsetting is it's happening to characters you like. Bone Tomahawk in particular is interesting, because—unlike something like From Dusk Till Dawn, which does a complete genre flip from crime film to vampire movie—it gradually devolves from a traditional-looking Western into a cannibal horror film. Almost as if the characters are traveling from one genre and entering into another (which is made clearer through the changing landscapes).

S. Craig Zahler is a unique writer and filmmaker who's able to tell stories across different mediums, but one never usurps the other when it comes to quality. When it comes to his takes on Westerns, the stories feel uniquely his own, but they don't seem like he's trying to deconstruct the genre or emulate the style with a modern twist (or have them take place in a modern setting). They feel like stories that he wanted to tell that just happened to take place in the Old West and didn't feel the need to go the way of paying homage.

We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful.

The first of Walmart's three major sales for Black Friday and Cyber Monday is now live, and there are already some amazing tech deals to take advantage of. I've gathered my top 10 tech products from the sale to make your life a little easier. For more, keep tabs on our Black Friday coverage, where we post the latest deals from not just Walmart, but Amazon, Best Buy, and other retailers' Black Friday deals.

Apple's latest smartwatch is the Series 12, but don't count out the Series 11. By sacrificing a few of Apple's newest features, you can save some money on the more premium version of this last-gen Apple Watch. Right now, the Titanium Series 11 GPS + cellular model is on sale for $429.

During WWDC 26 earlier this summer, Apple announced new Siri AI upgrades with watchOS 27—but only some Apple Watches have compatibility. Luckily, the Series 11 is one of them, at least for many of them. Some other upgrades in the new OS include a dedicated Siri app, a new app grid, a new single-tap gesture, among other features. Just note that only Series 12 and Ultra 4 can run Audio Intelligence.

The Garmin vivoactive 5 was $299.99 when it first came out in 2023 as their midrange lifestyle-focused fitness smartwatch. It features a 1.2-inch AMOLED touchscreen and an 11-day battery life (four to five days with the always-on display setting). You can get it for $169.99 right now. It's a great option for anyone looking to get into Garmin for the first time or upgrading from anything below it.

Bone conduction headphones are ideal for activities where it is vital to be able to hear your surroundings. They use a technology that sends audio vibrations to your inner ear while leaving your ear canals open. Shokz is one of, if not the best, brands making bone conduction headphones right now. At the high end of Shokz's offerings sit the OpenRun Pro 2, which impressed me when I tested them out for review. Walmart currently has a restored pair for $95 (originally $135.95 and $179.99 new).

They're $179 on Walmart as an early Black Friday deal, down from $249 and matching their lowest price ever.

Most, if not all, TV speakers aren't great. While you have plenty of options, the quickest and least expensive way to improve your TV's audio capabilities is to buy a soundbar. Compare a soundbar's size to the thin, small speakers jammed into modern TVs. The Vizio 4.1 Pro Soundbar and rear speakers come with Dolby Atmos support and cost just $79 (originally $148). They won't win any audio awards, but it's better than any built-in TV speakers, and for $79, it'll improve your experience without breaking the bank.

If you want to take things up a notch, consider this 5.1 channel sound system. Not only does it include far more channels than a single soundbar, but you're also adding a dedicated subwoofer to the mix. A subwoofer will make those thuds, explosions, and low vibrations much more pronounced than on a soundbar alone. For $149.99 (originally $249.99), you can get the ULTIMEA 5.1 surround sound system, which comes with a soundbar—replicating left, right, and center channels—two rear speakers, and a subwoofer.

#3397. 7 Fantasy Books To Read if You Love 'Percy Jackson & the Olympians'

Percy Jackson & the Olympians is a series of novels by American author Rick Riordan which was a massive success. The story is about Percy, a young boy who discovers he is a demigod, i.e. that his father was the Greek god Poseidon. He is then whisked away to a secluded camp in the wilderness, where other demigods train and learn to fight the ravenous monsters from Greek mythology that prowl the world, unseen by ordinary human eyes.

The series is perhaps most famous for its stellar Disney+ TV adaptation, as well as its disastrous early 2010s movies starring Logan Lerman. If you're a big fan of the book series and how they seamlessly blend 21st century life with mythology, there are plenty of other books out there that you might also wish to check out.

Tristan Strong Punches a Hole in the Sky is, admittedly, a bit of a mouthful. Lengthy title aside, this novel by Kwame Mbalia was actually presented and approved by Rick Riordan himself, basically linking the book with the legacy of Percy Jackson. The "Rick Riordan Presents" branding basically focuses on similar stories that feature mythological elements from various cultures that intersect with real life, and this tale is no exception to that rule.

Instead of being about Egyptian, Greco-Roman, or Norse mythology, which are arguably the most popular, this one features West African deities and folklore. This is combined with Black American folktales as well, creating a fascinating blended universe. The main character, the eponymous Tristan Strong, is actually incredibly likable. Plus, the story deserves points for bringing a mythology to life that rarely gets the chance to. Representing a rich, yet overlooked culture, combined with tween-friendly plotlines and lovable characters make this novel a real diamond in the rough. It's no wonder it was approved by the big man himself; you just can't beat that.

Caytlyn Brooke's Among the Hunted is the first novel in the Skyglass series, which is all about Greek mythology. It doesn't serve as a retelling of an existing narrative established in the mythos. Rather, it crafts a fresh story that is seamlessly integrated into the existing mythology, so that nothing feels out of place. As of yet, no other Skyglass books have been published, but it is implied that there are more on the way.

Among the Hunted centers on Kaitani, a nymph warrior who serves Olean. She has fallen in love with Hermes, the messenger of the gods, and is shouldering an unbearable guilt following the death of her closest friend. It's a horrible existence, made even worse by the fact that Zeus begins actively hunting Kaitani's sister. This causes her to embark on a quest for revenge, finally releasing the emotions she's been bottling up for 100 years. Now, she has just one goal: kill an immortal. This book is a bit more mature than typical YA novels, but it's still appropriate for teens and adults alike. If you're in this age group, and you love Percy Jackson and need some more Greek mythology, this is definitely something you should check out.

It might sound like a broken record to recommend this one, but Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone is still a great book for Percy Jackson fans. This is mainly due to the fact that Harry Potter basically revolutionized the whole YA genre, creating a market boom of similar stories, of which Percy Jackson was part of. However, the similarities go beyond surface-level trends, and go right down to the bones of each story.

Each series features a reluctant hero for a protagonist; a secluded, specialized academy for magical individuals; quippy dialogue; and various monsters from mythology. Both series have their fair share of adventure and comedy in equal measure. While Harry Potter doesn't feature any gods or deities from mythology, it has enough in common with Percy Jackson that it is often the next thing readers move on to when they've finished with Percy's story. In fact, many Potter fans also move straight on to Percy Jackson once they're finished.

The Serpent's Secret is the first in a series called Kiranmala and the Kingdom Beyond, a YA trilogy based on Bengali folklore. The eponymous protagonist, Kiranmala, is an ordinary 12-year-old living in New Jersey, who has been repeatedly told by her parents that she comes from a place outside this Earth, and that she is secretly an Indian princess. Though she never believes the stories, it turns out they were right, as she finds herself confronted by a horrifying rakkhosh demon, which abducts her parents. This is made more convoluted when two princes arrive and whisk her away to an alternate dimension.

Rather than being about Hinduism as a whole, the novel draws inspiration from lesser-talked about Indian traditions, imbuing its narrative with winged horses, talking birds, and a vengeful Serpent King. It's one of the most thematically interesting worlds told in a YA novel, and it fits in perfectly with the massive YA boom that began in the late '90s and peaked in the late 2000s/early 2010s. Fans of Percy Jackson will absolutely love this one, especially since it features ancient traditions and stories blending with aspects of real life in the 21st century.

Wolves is Book One of I Bring the Fire by C. Gockel. The book is primarily about Loki, the Norse god of trickery, and opens up with Loki waking up in a prison cell. This time, he has no idea what he's actually done to land himself there, but he does know one thing: his dear father, Odin, and brother, Thor, are up to something. Loki isn't sure what that something is, but he is sure that he doesn't like it one bit. Meanwhile, in a sleepy American Midwest town, a girl is on her way to her grandmother's house when her fate becomes intertwined with Loki's.

This hidden gem is perfectly suited for fans of Percy Jackson. After all, it has gods from a dead religion interacting with ordinary people and existing in the real world. The series also features the signature sass and chaos that Percy Jackson became famous for, alongside a cast of memorable characters and a grand adventure. It might not be the best book ever written, but it's something that fans of Percy Jackson will absolutely want to check out.

The Song of Achilles is a stand-alone novel that became a major hit with audiences. Written by Madeline Miller, this novel is a retelling of the Trojan War through the eyes of one of its most famed warriors, Achilles. Alongside Achilles is his lifelong friend, Patroclus, both of whom are trained by Chiron the centaur in the arts of warfare. When Helen of Sparta is kidnapped and the Greeks lay siege to Troy, Achilles and Patroclus answer the call. However, their relationship blossoms into something beyond friendship.

Indeed, the two do end up forming a romantic relationship, which was actually fairly commonplace in Ancient Greece. This book has a little bit of everything: there's romance, war, action, and adventure in equal measure, providing a fresh spin on an age-old story. The Song of Achilles won quite a few awards, including the Orange Prize for Fiction, one of the UK's most prestigious literary awards. If you're a teen or an adult, this book is an excellent recommendation for fans of Percy Jackson and the Olympians.

The Odyssey is the quintessential Greek myth, initially penned by Homer nearly 3,000 years ago. Rather than a novel, the book is formatted as an epic poem, which was a common storytelling medium at the time. While it wasn't technically considered fantasy when it first came out, it certainly fits the bill in hindsight. The story became so popular, even for the time, that it eventually became part of the official Greek canon, meaning it is an official part of Greek mythology.

Since the poem is one of the most famous things ever written, as well as one of the oldest surviving works of fiction, pretty much everybody knows the story by now. It's about a warrior named Odysseus who is returning home to Greece after spending years fighting in the Trojan War. This journey home is no easy feat, though, as Odysseus and his crew encounter numerous beasts and beings as they sail across the Greek islands. This is such an ideal pick for Percy Jackson fans because it's one of the main works that inspired it all in the first place. Fans will definitely recognize some of their favorite featured creatures from Riordan's series in the Odyssey, and will come to understand the origins of Greek epics.

#3396. A Number of Banks Are Experiencing Outages Right Now

If you're having trouble accessing your bank right now, you aren't alone. As of Monday afternoon, a number of banks are experiencing outages and interruptions to service.

That's according to Downdetector, which collects user reports of issues to different sites and services. As of this article, the site shows notable numbers of user reports with the following banks and credit companies: American Express, Ally, Bank of America, Capital One, Chase, Citi, Huntington Bank, JP Morgan, Navy Federal Credit Union, USAA, US Bank, and TD Bank, Visa, Wells Fargo. Even PayPal, Venmo, and Zelle, money-transferring services, are showing user reports as well.

There isn't a clear reason why these various companies are currently experiencing issues. The timing is suspicious, of course: These interruptions come after last week's massive Microsoft outage, which took down services like Outlook, Teams, and Microsoft 365. It also comes just days after the FAA unexpectedly grounded all flights in the U.S. There's no evidence there's any link between these events, but the frequency of these developments is concerning on the surface.

#3394. iOS 27.3 adds Siri AI usage limits, here’s what counts toward your limit

Earlier this week, Apple revealed that Siri AI usage limits will be implemented in iOS 27.3 and explained how iCloud+ increases those limits. Now we have a real-world example of what it looks like when limits are hit, and details on what counts toward those limits.

Siri AI and select other AI features will begin having usage limits in iOS 27.3 for advanced tasks.

This is standard practice with other AI services like ChatGPT, Gemini, and Claude because these tools rely on server-based models rather than running entirely on-device.

Here’s an example from the iOS 27.3 beta showing what it looks like when you hit your Siri AI daily usage limit. Per Ben in a post on X:

I hit my Siri AI usage limit, it still works though, including complex questions pic.twitter.com/XYYNPMnSnn

In a follow-up post, Ben clarifies that complex questions did stop working shortly after posting. As expected though, basic requests continued to work as usual—they don’t have a usage limit.

One question that Apple hasn’t made clear is what qualifies as a complex or “advanced” Siri AI request. The company shares just two examples of something advanced:

Suppose it gets it wrong like it does most of the time. I wonder if that still counts.

But leaker pdfu has discovered exactly the instructions Siri AI follows to determine whether a request counts as basic or advanced. In a post on X he outlines the parameters for requests deemed “advanced.”

Siri AI will check the request against this list, and if it involves any of these, it’s deemed “advanced.”

It would be helpful if Apple publicly documented these guidelines for users. But perhaps after iOS 27.3 ships and usage limits are fully implemented, we’ll get more detail from the company.

#3393. 10 Books Like ‘Dungeon Crawler Carl’ You Should Read Next

Jeff Somers is a freelancer who has been writing about writing, books, personal finance, and home maintenance since 2012.

Jeff has published nine novels and more than 70 short stories; his story Ringing the Changes was selected for inclusion in The Best American Mystery Stories 2006. In 2018, Jeff published the book Writing Without Rules: How to Write & Sell a Novel Without Guidelines, Experts, or (Occasionally) Pants. He holds a bachelor’s degree in English and previously worked in medical publishing as a production editor.

When not writing, Jeff spends his free time fixing up his old house. He has tackled a wide range of DIY projects, including remodeling a bathroom entirely on his own in two weeks, and building a roof deck that hasn't fallen down yet. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

There’s nothing quite like Dungeon Crawler Carl, Matt Dinniman’s hilarious, inventive, and surprisingly emotional book series about a man in his underwear forced to fight his way through a livestreamed game show based on dungeon-crawling video games that takes place after an alien takeover of Earth. (Did I mention he's accompanied by his ex-girlfriend’s suddenly talkative cat?)

The premise should not work, but it sure does—and it makes more sense if you know it fits into a popular genre known as "LitRPG," a blend of "literature" and "role-playing game." If you've torn through all eight books released so far and you're looking for more reads that blend surprisingly deep hilarity with tabletop and video game rules (or just similar feels), here are 10 books you should check out.

An isekai story that lands in the sweet spot for DCC fans, He Who Fights with Monsters kicks off with Jason—a completely normal, kind of boring middle manager—waking up in a strange hedge maze, completely nude (even his hair is gone). He has magic that works like a video game, and has to deal with quests that slowly give him clothes (it’s a relief when he finally acquires some pants), force him to survive cannibals, and hunt down various monsters that definitely need killing. It’s got the same “gaming rules” structure as DCC and a similarly absurdist tone, with just the right spice of darkness.

The Cradle series by Will Wight isn’t a LitRPG, and it doesn’t have Carl’s focus on humor, but it’s another progression fantasy with enough game-like elements to be a great match. Lindon is an “unsouled,” incapable of gaining any of the sacred arts and doomed to a life without a future. His lack of power makes Lindon ferociously determined to find an alternative path to power and success, and that’s what drives this story. He has to find creative ways to move forward, and slowly this leads him to a path that just might make him the most powerful person in his world. DCC fans will love the progression and the tone.

One of the key elements of any video game is the respawn—you get killed, but you pop back up to try again, sometimes at the beginning, sometimes at a save point. Django Wexler leverages that mechanic to great effect in How to Become the Dark Lord and Die Trying. Davi has been summoned to a fantasy world to be the hero, the person who defeats the Dark Lord and saves the day—but she’s failed (and died) so many times, she’s fed up, and decides that on this run through, she’s going to switch sides and become the Dark Lord, using all her knowledge gained from endless replays to her advantage. The humor is pitch-black the way DCC fans like it, and the progressive structure is a perfect fit.

Is Princess Donut your favorite part of Dungeon Crawler Carl? Of course she is. In that case, check out Andrew Seiple’s Threadbare series. Threadbare is a stuffed bear brought to magical life in a failed experiment. He’s a foot tall, full of stuffing, and extremely dumb when the story begins. But when he’s rescued by a little girl and plunged into a horrible series of dangers, Threadbare has to find a way to level up. Like DCC, Threadbare starts off leaning into the absurdity and humor, then slowly gains emotional gravitas as the story progresses.

If you play tabletop RPGs, you’ve encountered a Murderhobo or two: A character who solves all their problems by killing—even members of their own party. Luke doesn’t aspire to be a Murderhobo—he just wants to take over the family business and hang with his buddies. But when an invasion threatens the kingdom, everyone over the age of 17 is ordered to be tested for Potential. Luke’s friends all test high and join the Ascender Corps, traveling to different planes for training. Luke tests ... very low, and when he steps through a portal to engage in his training, he finds himself without any guidance or training in a strange, deadly world where his only chance of survival is to murder his way through it. It’s dark, darkly funny, and a progression fantasy like no other.

If you’re looking for a book series that combines the dark, chaotic humor, absurd game mechanics, and surprising emotional depth of Carl, here’s Ryan “Quicksave” Romano, a man who has the unique ability to literally create a save point in his existence that allows him to go back and redo things whenever he dies. Searching for a childhood friend, he becomes embroiled in a violent gang war that lets him make good use of his power—but underneath the snark and the insanity of Ryan’s existence is a surprisingly affecting story of a man who has suffered, and suffered countless tragedies that are definitely taking their toll.

If your fave bit of DCC is Carl himself—a mediocre dude in an extraordinary situation—you should read Dennis E. Taylor’s fantastic Bobiverse books. Bob is a software engineer who hits it big and promptly dies, waking up to discover a century has passed and he’s been repurposed as an AI controlling a space probe searching for new planets for humanity to inhabit. If he fails in his mission (and he’s not the only probe out there), he’ll be turned off for good. Luckily, he can make copies of himself, and he’s pretty smart. The humor here is smart and soaked in pop culture, making it a perfect match for DCC fans.

Want more of Carl’s absurdist humor? Mayor of Noobtown is the LitRPG you’re looking for. Jim dies and wakes up in a video game-esque universe and finds himself stuck in the zone designated for newbies—players with no experience, skill, or hope. The area fell out of the mainline progression mechanic a long time ago, so there doesn’t seem to be a way to gain power, and the monsters are not at all concerned about the unfairness of it all, so Jim has to figure out how to advance in a universe that seems designed to kill him (again).

If you want to lean into the meta side of things, check out Scathing Reviewer, written by an author who goes by the unusual pen name "BananaDragon." Liu Peijin is the author of a sprawling LitRPG web novel, and she’s used to the bad reviews and complaints from readers—and quite combative about it. When her books’ universe blossoms into a very dangerous new reality, she should be perfectly positioned to survive, having written the story in the first place. But her story becoming real also means her insufferable protagonist is real, and all those nasty critics are now passing judgment on her entire existence. It’s a dark, funny takedown of the entire genre itself, and DCC fans will love it.

If you want a story that parallels the dungeon crawling aspect of DCC, Andrew Rowe’s Arcane Ascension series is the ticket. The Serpent Spire is a tower of constantly changing traps, puzzles, and dangerous creatures. If you enter and survive, you emerge with magical powers. Corin Cadence’s brother entered the Serpent Spire years ago and never returned—and now Corin is determined not only to survive, but to make it to the top, where legend says a goddess will grant you whatever you wish. And what Corin wants is his brother back. It’s a literal progression combined with LitRPG rules, game-inspired puzzle-solving, and a complex magic system that fans of Carl will definitely enjoy.

#3389. Assassin's Creed: Echoes Of The Past Officially Releasing December 2026

Since the launch of Assassin's Creed in 2007, the stealth-action series from Ubisoft has become one of the cornerstones of gaming, and with fourteen mainline entries now under its belt, it is safe to say that it is here to stay.

Taking players across the globe, and exploring multiple eras, movements, and cultures, Assassin's Creed has been the best history teacher we could have had, and to celebrate the franchise approaching its 20th anniversary, Assassin's Creed: Echoes of the Past is set to stun us all when it arrives this December.

Courtesy of the artist collective Les 7 Doigts, Heredis: Echoes of the Past is a live show that takes fans to the Ubisoft universe with an experience that combines both theater and circus. Oh, and of course, there will also be plenty of parkour.

Whilst a preview will be held on 3 December 2026, at the Maisonneuve Theater in Montreal, several performances will be scheduled between January 21 and February 7, 2027, and so you have plenty of time to grab your tickets. So, what can you expect?

A troop of acrobats will take to the stage to perform some incredible stunts, with the show itself expected to last two hours. However, the storyline will focus on a young man called Naël who, after receiving a letter on his 25th birthday, will find his destiny changed forever. As such, he will have to embark on a journey to discover the mystery behind his father's appearance, an event that he refuses to accept.

Featuring an original Assassin's Creed storyline, Heredis: Echoes of the Past will see Naël join the HEREDIS program, and through this, he will be able to travel through many historical eras which echo the ones we all know and love from the Assassin's Creed franchise so far. Not only that, but with the stage show being officially supported by Ubisoft, you can expect a truly spectacular experience with the creator's stamp of approval.

Despite featuring nods to the games, such as in the historical periods that are covered, it will not focus on any of the games. As such, even those unfamiliar with the franchise will be able to go and watch. However, the catch here is that, unless you can make the Montreal preview, you will need to head to the Casino de Paris, France.

Over on r/assassinscreed, fans discussed the upcoming stage show, and took to the comments to share their thoughts. One user shared, "One of the theater companies I work with presented one of 7Fingers’ shows a year or so before I started working there, and they were pretty well-attended shows. We are thinking of bringing them back to present another of their works, hopefully in the next few years. I really hope 7Fingers is able to bring Heredis to more than just Canada and France!" Another shared, "This actually sounds incredible to be honest."

So, if you find yourself in Canada or France and just so happen to be an Assassin's Creed fan, make sure to check out Heredis: Echoes of the Past and partake in an original experience you will never forget.

#3387. 8 Thrillers That Become Masterpieces in the Last 30 Minutes

Audiences seek movies as a temporary escape from reality, yet they challenge their minds and send a tingle down their spines. A good thriller triggers a cinematic fight-or-flight from the safety of your seat. They get to play along, becoming active participants as they try to outsmart the plot, crack the mystery, or guess the villain's motives before the reveal.

Some great thrillers start off strong but end with a whimper. Then there are those that become legendary masterpieces within the final 30 minutes. From shocking twists you never saw coming to terrifying revelations that reshape the entire narrative, these 10 thriller films leave a lasting impression long after the final credits roll.

Directed by David Fincher and written by Gillian Flynn, Gone Girl became the definitive domestic psychological thriller. The story follows Nick Dunne (Ben Affleck) as he becomes the prime suspect in the sudden disappearance of his wife, Amy (Rosamund Pike), on their fifth wedding anniversary. As the police and media circus close in, a series of dark twists reveals that neither spouse is who they appear to be, exposing a deeply toxic and manipulative marriage.

Rather than ending with a neat resolution, the climax traps the characters in a dark, satirical commentary on modern marriage and media manipulation. Amy’s return home isn't a relief; it is a life sentence for Nick. By using her pregnancy to lock him into the marriage, Amy ensures total control, turning the happy ending into a satire. Gone Girl's final minutes expose their marriage as a performance, with both partners actively playing a role for public consumption, while Trent Reznor and Atticus Ross' score provides a false sense of calm.

David Lynch's masterpiece Mulholland Drive is a gem from the start of the 21st century. The surreal thriller follows an aspiring actress, Betty (Naomi Watts), who helps an amnesiac woman, Rita (Laura Harring), piece together her identity after a car crash in Los Angeles. The story fractures into a dark, dreamlike puzzle that blurs the line between Hollywood fantasy and a tragic, guilt-ridden reality.

In the final 30 minutes, Lynch transforms the movie from a strange neo-noir mystery into a devastating psychological portrait, turning a surreal thriller into a raw, heartbreaking tragedy about loneliness and self-destruction. The pastel glamour is ripped away to reveal the raw, grim reality of Diane Selwyn, a depressed, failed actress consumed by jealousy, unrequited love, and crushing guilt. Lynch reframes the entire movie as a study of how people use romantic illusions, denial, and fantasy to escape personal failure and moral decay.

Directed and co-written by Park Chan-wook, the South Korean action thriller Oldboy follows Oh Dae-su (Choi Min-sik), who, after being mysteriously kidnapped and imprisoned in a single room for 15 years, is suddenly released and given five days to track down his captor and uncover the motive behind his torment. His quest for vengeance leads him down a dark path of shocking revelations and devastating secrets.

A truly diabolical story, Oldboy transforms a brutal revenge thriller into an epic tragedy, shifting the story from physical violence to total psychological devastation. Dae-su fights through conspiracies and brutal hand-to-hand corridors, expecting a typical action-hero resolution: the hero kills the villain and wins. Instead, we have something far more twisting and crueler. In the final snowy sequence, the lingering, ambiguous look on the protagonist's face shows that trauma cannot simply be excised; instead, it's something one must learn to accept or else be consumed by it.

In Prisoners, directed by Denis Villeneuve, the story follows Keller Dover (Hugh Jackman) as he desperately searches for his young daughter and her friend after they go missing on Thanksgiving. When Detective Loki (Jake Gyllenhaal) releases the prime suspect, Alex Jones (Paul Dano), for lack of evidence, Dover takes matters into his own hands, pushing moral boundaries as a dedicated detective races against time to solve the mystery.

The grim, gripping drama unravels as the complex moral framework builds to an intense, clock-ticking climax that recontextualizes everything that came before. After a series of wrong choices, Keller is trapped in the secret pit—the very place his daughter was kept, forced to face the literal and spiritual hole he dug for himself. Loki stands in the freezing cold, hearing the faint sound of Anna’s red whistle from the ground, leaving Keller’s rescue uncertain. With a perfectly ambiguous ending, we are left to decide whether he deserves salvation after the atrocities he committed.​​​​​​​

Few films elicit guttural reactions quite like Se7en. Directed by David Fincher, the psychological crime drama follows two homicide detectives, William Somerset (Morgan Freeman), a veteran nearing retirement, and David Mills (Brad Pitt), his new, hot-headed partner, as they track a meticulous serial killer (Kevin Spacey), who uses the seven deadly sins as motifs for his gruesome murders.

Se7en becomes an exceptionally dark police procedural by subverting classic Hollywood tropes, shifting power psychologically, and delivering a devastatingly bleak moral conclusion. John Doe turns himself in, halting the “catch the killer” momentum. Thrust into a bright, vast, and barren desert landscape under harsh daylight, the protagonists are exposed as Doe dominates the action. The movie ends with the antagonist successfully completing his horrific masterpiece, leaving the audience with an overwhelming sense of dread.

Scorsese’s crime thriller The Departed follows Billy Costigan Jr. (DiCaprio), an undercover cop who infiltrates an Irish gang, and Colin Sullivan (Matt Damon), a mole within the police department who secretly works for the gang's kingpin. Both sides eventually realize a traitor lurks in their ranks, sparking a deadly, high-stakes race for each man to uncover the other's identity before his own is exposed.

In the final thirty minutes, The Departed delivers a relentless, breathless cascade of subversion, consequences, and brutal payoffs. Right when audiences expect a traditional cinematic confrontation between Costigan and Sullivan, the movie pulls the rug out. Sergeant Dignam (Mark Wahlberg) acts as a silent instrument of pure karma, delivering a deeply satisfying yet bleakly cynical conclusion. The final, poetic shot of a literal rat scurrying across Sullivan's balcony acts as punctuation: corruption is foundational, the system is deeply broken, and the cycle of duplicity survives long after the players are dead.​​​​​​​

The Prestige may be one of Christopher Nolan's most quintessential films. Set in 19th-century London, the story centers on two rival stage magicians, Robert Angier (Jackman) and Alfred Borden (Christian Bale), who engage in a bitter, obsessive feud to create the ultimate illusion. Their fierce competition escalates into a dangerous game of sabotage and deceit, costing them everything they hold dear.

Established as a magic trick, the film’s final act executes a perfect structural "Prestige"—the final stage of a magic trick where everything hidden is dramatically revealed. The opening monologue by Cutter (Michael Caine) explaining the Pledge, the Turn, and the Prestige is the blueprint for the entire film. Ultimately, as they try to destroy each other, Borden loses his brother and the woman he loved, while Angier loses his humanity entirely. The Prestige is a brilliant revenge thriller with an unforgettable gut-punch of an ending.

Directed by Bryan Singer, The Usual Suspects follows five criminals who meet during a routine police lineup and plan a heist, only to be blackmailed by a mysterious, legendary crime lord named Keyser Söze. The entire story is told through the interrogation and flashbacks of the sole survivor of a subsequent, bloody boat explosion, Verbal Kint (Spacey).

The final revelation remains one of cinema's greatest endings, reconfiguring the thriller into a masterclass in psychological manipulation and the malleability of truth. The final sequence reveals that Verbal fabricated the entire story on the spot using random objects sitting on Kujan's office bulletin board and desk. As Verbal walks out of the precinct, drops his limp, and lights a cigarette, the film cuts back through the previous 90 minutes. Every little aspect here is designed to mislead. Verbal played the part so effectively that the hunter sat across from the devil the whole time without ever noticing.

ChatGPT dictation is getting a boost today. OpenAI has updated the speech-to-text feature with Live Dictation that improves both speed and reliability. The enhanced dictation update also removes the 10-minute limit.

“Dictation in ChatGPT is getting faster and more reliable,” OpenAI announced on X.

Dictation in ChatGPT is getting faster and more reliable.

With Live Dictation, your speech turns into text as you talk, so you spend less time waiting for your message to finish transcribing. Tap or click on the waveform to show or hide text as you go. We’ve also removed the 10-minute recording limit.

Live Dictation is rolling out globally to all ChatGPT plans on iOS, Android, web, and the desktop app.

#3380. HBO's 9-Part Thriller Masterpiece Has Earned Its Status As A Modern Classic

There was a time when superhero TV shows were synonymous with colorful costumes, campy action, and plots that focused much more on outlandish spectacle than delivering anything grounded or relatable. The genre has, thankfully, developed a grittier and more realistic edge in the age of streaming. Modern superhero series like The Penguin, Daredevil: Born Again, and Lanterns have ditched the obsession with superpowered spectacle to instead focus on the injustices and inequality that lead to heroes taking up their mantles in the first place.

That approach to small-screen superhero stories feels familiar in the 2020s, but this definitely wasn’t always the case. The prestige superhero series model didn’t come out of nowhere, either. There’s a show that paved the way for contemporary hits that give the genre its current level of dramatic clout and mainstream respect among those who’d once never have given a superhero story a chance. That series is 2019’s Watchmen, HBO’s sequel miniseries to Alan Moore’s groundbreaking graphic novel.

Set in Tulsa 34 years after the attack on New York in Alan Moore’s original story, Watchmen introduces viewers to detective Angela Abar (Regina King) as she investigates a white supremacist group. The case draws her into the lives of the original Watchmen vigilantes while continuing the graphic novel’s questioning of whether wearing a mask and calling oneself a hero is enough to make it true. While it may not be a superhero household name, shows like The Penguin, Lanterns, and Daredevil: Born Again may not ever have existed without HBO’s Watchmen to pave the way.

While there were several grittier superhero shows arriving around the same time as Watchmen, such as The Boys in the same year or the Netflix-Marvel shows that began with Daredevil in 2015, none of them felt like they changed the game in quite the same way as HBO’s miniseries. For years, the selling points of pretty much every superhero TV show were its hero, its villain, and the prospect of seeing them fight. Watchmen bucked this trend in a way few, if any, series had before.

Rather than focusing on setting up a hero-villain showdown, HBO’s Watchmen built itself around a mystery. It didn’t feel like a superhero show. It felt like a detective show that just so happened to have superheroes in it. What’s more, these “heroes” are far from morally good. Watchmen presents its masked vigilantes not as saviors, but as ordinary people with their own ideological agendas. It’s an approach that put a fresh spin on the familiar tropes of the genre. For example, secret identities shift from being a way for heroes to protect their loved ones to a way to use anonymity to negate accountability.

Opening with the 1921 Tulsa Race Massacre also gave Watchmen a sense of history and political relevance that superhero TV series rarely attempted at the time. By the time the action reaches 2019, generations have grown up with different ideas about what a hero is and who deserves their protection. Who counts as a hero and a villain depends on perspective, with those that society labels as the former often working to hold up corrupt institutions and protect a societal status quo that perpetuates inequality.

That shift from the traditional hero-vs-villain setup to a politically charged mystery narrative won Watchmen no shortage of acclaim, including 11 Primetime Emmy wins. At the time, a superhero series receiving this much critical praise was basically unheard of. It was a true turning point for the genre on the small screen. Many gritty and grounded superhero TV shows have followed in the years since, but none have made as much of an impact on the genre itself quite like Watchmen.

While Watchmen is celebrated today and was far from a ratings flop when it aired in 2019, it didn’t perform as well as it could have done given just how good it is. The reasons why are obvious, too. While it’s an incredible piece of television in its own right, early discussions about Watchmen were defined not by its merits, but by its relation to the source material. Alan Moore’s Watchmen comics are among the most beloved of all time. As is often the case with such highly regarded properties, HBO’s adaptation became defined by the divisive and often toxic responses of the existing fandom.

Even the announcement that HBO was creating a sequel to Watchmen was met with immediate and disproportionately vocal backlash. Many fans of the original graphic novel wanted Alan Moore’s story to stand alone. This wasn’t just down to longtime fans wanting the existing canon and timeline to remain untouched, either. There were also some particularly toxic and abhorrent reactions to racism becoming central to HBO’s story too. For casual viewers who weren’t at all familiar with the Watchmen comic, the discussions surrounding the 2019 miniseries made it seem like a hotbed of controversy that it simply wasn’t worth wading into.

This is an incredible shame, because Watchmen is an incredibly solid thriller that even viewers completely unaware of Alan Moore’s original graphic novel are bound to appreciate. It’s not just a game-changing superhero TV series, it’s a rich mystery story that uses its genre as a tool to explore some incredibly poignant themes and topics. While it’s impossible to say for certain, it feels likely that Watchmen would today be much more widely discussed if its legacy wasn't defined by the polarizing pop-culture discourse that surrounded it when it arrived in 2019.
