Amazon's Black Friday 2026 sale has brought the Sonos Arc Ultra down to $849 from its usual $1,099, a $250 discount that marks its lowest price yet. PCMag named it the best soundbar of 2024 and gave it an “outstanding” rating in its review. Still, $849 is a lot to spend on a single soundbar, and anyone shopping on a tighter budget will find more affordable picks in our Fire TV soundbar roundup. For more editor-vetted tech deals, check out our comprehensive Black Friday coverage.

For those who can make room in their budget, the next thing to plan around is space, since the Arc Ultra measures a little over 46 inches across and weighs about 13 pounds, making it a natural match for a larger TV. Despite all that width, it keeps a low profile at just under three inches tall, so it can sit beneath most screens without blocking the picture, or you can wall-mount it if you would rather keep your TV stand clear. All that size makes room for a 9.1.4-channel layout (a big step up from the original Arc) that gives Dolby Atmos effects more space to spread around and above you. Sonos also added a new Sound Motion driver that it says doubles the original Arc's bass, giving action scenes real weight without a separate subwoofer, though you can still add a Sub 4 later for more rumble.

At the other end of the sound spectrum, voices and dialogue come through clearly even at low volumes, and a Speech Enhancement mode lifts them further. Trueplay tuning then adjusts the sound to your room, with a quick version on Android and iOS and a more detailed one for iPhone owners. The biggest drawback is connectivity, since the Arc Ultra has a single HDMI eARC port with no passthrough, which can leave you short on inputs for a console or streaming box, and no optical port. It also lacks DTS:X support, a letdown for some Blu-ray collectors, and voice control is limited to Alexa or Sonos' own assistant, though Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, and AirPlay 2 make streaming music from your phone easy.

In short, yes, Black Friday still offers discounts that can be rare throughout the rest of the year. If there’s something you want to buy, or you’re shopping for gifts, it’s a good time to look for discounts on what you need, especially tech sales, home improvement supplies, and fitness tech. Of course, if you need to save money, the best way to save is not to buy anything.

Follow our Black Friday coverage for the latest and best deals our team finds. Another good tip is to only buy what you need. It sounds simple, but making a list of the things you want before jumping into a sale with millions of products helps you focus and make smarter decisions.

The best thing you can do is compare the prices with other retailers that have Black Friday sales. If that seems like too much work, you can just follow our Black Friday coverage (we're already doing all the searching and vetting for you). Some other tips are making sure you're not being sold an older or cheaper version and always reading reviews.

#3252. Ina Garten Reveals Why She Will Never Do ‘Dancing With The Stars’

Celebrity Chef Ina Garten revealed this week on her Happy Hour podcast that she once turned down Dancing with the Stars.

Discussing fear, overcoming it and whether she had ever turned something down because it was “too scary,” Garten said, “I think I absolutely have…Somebody asked me to do Dancing with the Stars. I thought nobody needs to see that. That’s not happening.”

The chef-turned-podcaster explained, “I thought the closer I got to the day when I had to do it, the more I’d have nightmares. I feel like a lot of people would feel like that. I don’t know. That’s so intimidating.”

Guest Rose Byrne agreed, ‘I would be terrified of that.” Watch on Deadline

Numerous other celebrity chefs have competed on the ABC show, including Rocco DiSpirito, Paula Deen and Giada De Laurentiis, the latter of whom broke her toe while practicing for this season.

Despite her resistance to doing the cha-cha on TV, Garten said that generally she’s “made peace with fear,” given that she often finds herself out over her skis.

“If you push yourself enough, then you have to figure out how to deal with fear. I mean, I feel like um it’s always with me. I never get rid of it. It’s like in the side car next to me while I’m going along.”

The Dancing with the Stars finale will air live coast-to-coast for the first time on Tuesday.

#3251. How Do You Land on a Moon With Almost No Gravity?

Japan’s MMX mission aims to sample the Martian moon Phobos

Japan's MMX spacecraft will fire its engines to slow down and enter orbit around Mars.

Last August, looking up from the edge of an ancient river delta on Mars, the Perseverance rover’s electronic eye spied an oblong shadow crossing the distant, glowing Sun. Phobos, the Martian moon named for the Greek god of fear and panic, was transiting the solar disk. Too small to darken the pale, dust-tinged sky, but orbiting close enough to eclipse a significant fraction of the Sun, Phobos passed in less than a minute.

NASA’s Perseverance rover captured Phobos passing in front of the Sun from the surface of Mars.ASU/MSSS/SSI/JPL-Caltech/NASA

The tiny moon, with its murky origins, is an enigma, and one whose makeup and history could tell us much about Mars and the wider solar system. And now the international Martian Moons eXploration (MMX) mission, which successfully launched on 20 October, seeks to explore that mystery with an unprecedented series of landings on the unknown surface of Phobos.

This mission brings unusual challenges—for example, designing an orbit to study a microgravity moon orbiting a much larger planet. Engineers also had to figure out how to assess and land on this low-gravity pile of loosely assembled dirt and rock, how a rover might rove across it, and how the spacecraft might take samples and return them to Earth.

“I often say that landing on Phobos is like trying to land a balloon,” says Yasuhiro Kawakatsu, project manager of MMX at the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA). “It’s very difficult to drop a balloon to the ground and prevent it from tilting or bouncing.”

Phobos is one of two small Martian moons; the other is Deimos, named after the Greek god of dread and terror. Their cosmic origins are unknown, though there are two prevailing theories. One holds that the moons were once asteroids from the belt between Mars and Jupiter, captured by the smaller planet’s gravity. In the other theory, Phobos and Deimos formed when a large celestial body slammed into Mars, sending debris into orbit. Some models suggest the pair are the last survivors from a cluster of satellites.

The enormous Stickney crater, roughly 9 kilometers across, dominates this view of Phobos taken by NASA’s Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter.University of Arizona/JPL-Caltech/NASA

Scientifically speaking, Phobos is considered a rubble pile, a loosely consolidated aggregate of rock and dust. Far too small to become spherical under its own mass, it’s shaped like a lumpy potato, roughly 27 kilometers in length, with only 1/1,800th of Earth’s gravity. On Phobos, a typical adult would weigh about as much as a tennis ball does on Earth.

More than 10 years in the making, MMX launched on Japan’s flagship H3 rocket from Tanegashima spaceport on 20 October local time. It will arrive at Mars in 2027 carrying scientific payloads from several space agencies, including NASA, and a new rover called Idefix developed by the French and German space agencies (CNES and DLR) in collaboration with JAXA.

Engineers assembled MMX’s modules at Japan’s Tanegashima Space Center before the spacecraft’s October 2026 launch.JAXA

MMX consists of three modules: a propulsion module to power its journey to Mars and apply the brakes to enter orbit around the red planet; an exploration module carrying the rover, sampling gear, and other scientific instruments; and a return module, attached to the exploration module, that harbors the capsule destined for a high-speed reentry into Earth’s atmosphere. After collecting samples on Phobos, the exploration and return modules will lift off together. The exploration module will then be jettisoned while the return module sets a course back home.

If all goes according to plan, MMX will deliver a 10-gram sample to Earth in the second half of 2031. But the mission will face a series of daunting challenges to reach that end point, including navigating complex orbits around Phobos and landing on its surface while Mars periodically blocks communications with Earth.

The MMX’s modular design includes the propulsion module [left] and the exploration and return modules [right].Kyodo News/Getty Images

“It’s the most complex mission I have ever seen,” says Patrick Michel, director of research at CNRS (the French National Center for Scientific Research) and co-principal investigator on Idefix.

An H3 rocket carried MMX into space on 20 October 2026, beginning the mission’s five-year journey to Phobos and back.The Asahi Shimbun/Getty Images

Once MMX reached low Earth orbit, its propulsion module’s engine fired, kicking off a nearly year-long deep-space cruise to Mars. On arrival, the spacecraft will need to fire its engines in an extended, carefully timed burn to slow down enough to be captured by Mars gravity. The propulsion module will then be jettisoned, leaving the exploration and return modules to orbit Mars.

“If something doesn’t go according to plan, MMX will fly by Mars and get catapulted into the solar system,” says Nicola Baresi, an astrodynamicist who coauthored a paper on specially designed orbits for MMX.

From that initial orbit, MMX will transition into a specially designed quasi-satellite orbit that allows it to keep pace with the small moon but also move around it. Since Phobos is too small to orbit in the conventional sense, the spacecraft will orbit Mars alongside the moon, following a clever egg-shaped path that slings MMX alternately ahead of and behind the moon. “When you’re closer to Mars, you’re accelerating with respect to Phobos, and when you’re farther from Mars, you’re decelerating. So you essentially go back and forth,” explains Baresi.

Martian Maneuvers To reach Phobos, MMX will execute three major maneuvers: MOI-1 will put the spacecraft into orbit around Mars, MOI-2 will transfer it toward Phobos, and MOI-3 will place it into its final orbit alongside the moon.Chris Philpot

To reach Phobos, MMX will execute three major maneuvers: MOI-1 will put the spacecraft into orbit around Mars, MOI-2 will transfer it toward Phobos, and MOI-3 will place it into its final orbit alongside the moon.

The best existing images of Phobos, from spacecraft such as NASA’s Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter and ESA’s Mars Express, have resolutions of only a few meters per pixel. That’s larger than Idefix, the mission’s rover, itself about the size of a microwave oven. To map the surface in greater detail, MMX will loop in front of and behind Phobos at distances ranging from 200 kilometers to less than 20 km from the surface.

During its two-year remote sensing campaign, the exploration module will use several cameras and a laser altimeter to map the surface in high resolution and look for candidate landing sites. When Mars passes behind the Sun as seen from the Earth, causing a roughly two-week communications blackout, MMX will retreat into a larger, stable orbit. After communications resume, MMX will prepare to send its first visitor down to the surface.

Before the exploration and connected return modules attempt to land, Kawakatsu says, MMX will send a scout that in Japanese is called “the first penguin,” leaping into unknown waters. For this mission, the first to leap will be the Idefix rover, named for the canine companion to Obelix in the French comics series Asterix. The exploration module will release the rover during a low-altitude pass of between 40 and 100 meters above Phobos’s surface in 2028 or early 2029.

MMX will use its TENGOO camera [left] and LIDAR laser altimeter [right] to map Phobos’s terrain.JAXA

It will be a tense moment that calls back to 2005, during Japan’s Hayabusa mission to explore the asteroid Itokawa. In a similarly designed drop, the MINERVA rover was released from an orbiter, but erroneously at 200 meters instead of the intended 70 meters. The rover missed the asteroid and, without propulsion, drifted off into deep space.

Idefix will get a slight nudge out of the exploration module toward its negligible-gravity target, freefalling and likely tumbling as it goes. It’s expected to touch down with a velocity of less than 1 meter per second. Unlike rovers that have landed on other surfaces with airbags or dedicated landing legs, Idefix will land without protection, apart from some extra padding on the solar panels due to their critical nature. The barely-there gravity of Phobos should allow the 23-kilogram rover to land softly, though exactly how this landing will play out is hard to predict.

The Idefix rover will travel to Phobos with its wheels tucked in and solar panels folded.DLR

“It will bounce probably several times,” says Stephan Ulamec, Idefix’s co-principal investigator and project manager at DLR. “It will come to rest somehow in some position.” Once it’s still, four retracted legs will deploy to right the rover autonomously, regardless of its orientation. It will then unfold its solar panels to charge its batteries for exploration tasks ahead.

A simulation shows how Idefix is expected to tumble onto Phobos, right itself using its articulated legs, and begin exploring the moon’s surface. DLR

Once operational, Idefix will roll at a snail’s pace, topping out at one millimeter per second. Its metal wheels have protruding blades like a paddle wheel, designed to gain traction in Phobos’s microgravity. “If we were to drive our rover faster, then it would actually be more like we were swimming through instead of driving across the surface,” says Cecily Sunday, a doctoral student involved in testing Idefix’s WheelCams at the Institut Superieur de l’Aeronautique et de l’Espace (ISAE-Supaéro) in Toulouse, France.

The WheelCams, a pair of cameras placed on the underside of the rover, will observe the wheels and their tracks during Idefix’s planned 100-Earth-day primary mission. The images will help researchers study the size and distribution of grains in Phobos’s regolith and how cohesive they are. How much or how little the grains stick together will greatly impact how Idefix moves. Sunday likens this to the difference between driving on dry and wet sand. “Think of trying to build a sandcastle with dry sand,” she says. “You can’t. Add water, and suddenly you can.”

The Idefix rover was mounted between the MMX spacecraft’s landing legs for the journey to Phobos.DLR

The team tested the rover’s nine-bladed wheels on a variety of materials, including Phobos regolith simulants provided by JAXA and DLR, lunar simulants, glass beads, quartz sand, and clay pebbles. “We characterize the mechanical properties of each simulant precisely, then test across the full range, with varying grain size, angularity, and even color, so we can map what we see in the WheelCam images back to actual surface properties,” Sunday says.

Despite the microgravity and Phobos’s rubble-pile nature, Sunday says Earth-based tests can approximate the rover’s motion on the surface of the small moon fairly well. While Phobos’s reduced gravity lowers the rover’s effective weight, there is also reduced pressure between the grains beneath its wheels. “As long as you’re moving very, very slowly and using the same materials and the same weight of the system, they should be representative,” Sunday says.

With four paddle-like wheels and deployable solar panels, Idefix is designed to crawl across Phobos.Ardan Fuessmann/Imago/Alamy

Idefix’s interactions with its new home will offer “sub-millimeter resolution and information on porosity, on grain size, on surface strength, on how hard is the material,” Ulamec says. “It fills a gap between remote observations from orbit and detailed observations of the return samples back on Earth.”

What Idefix finds on this rocky, rugged world will help determine how and where JAXA attempts to land the main spacecraft. Michel says the touchdown will provide ground truth for understanding of Phobos. When NASA’s OSIRIS-REx spacecraft touched down on the asteroid Bennu to collect a sample, its sampling arm surprisingly sank nearly half a meter into the loose material. But Ulamec doesn’t think Idefix will sink deep into Phobos, noting that Bennu is very different and much smaller, with a diameter of 500 meters.

Once Idefix has investigated the surface, MMX will face an even greater challenge: landing its much larger exploration module on Phobos. The spacecraft will make a controlled descent to roughly 10 meters above the surface, then drop the remaining distance in free fall. With so little gravity to pull it downward, even a small sideways motion could cause the lander to tip or bounce away. A successful, upright landing would mark the start of up to two hours on Phobos for the crucial sampling phase.

The MMX mission draws on the experience and technologies of Japan’s two Hayabusa sample-return missions, which landed on the asteroids Itokawa and Ryugu. But this mission has many more moving parts. MMX’s exploration module will use two sampling devices—a coring sampler developed by JAXA and a pneumatic sampler provided by NASA and fabricated by Honeybee Robotics, a subsidiary of Blue Origin. Data from these tools, and those carried by the Idefix rover, could answer questions about the origin of Phobos and how the Mars system has evolved.

The coring sampler uses a robot arm and a cylindrical corer designed to reach at least 2 centimeters below the surface. The arm can maneuver to find the best site for digging. “That by itself is a challenge because we’ve never done it,” Michel says. “You never know what can happen at the very sampling site itself, where you might have a boulder and the arm cannot move.”

Probing beneath the top layer will be valuable because solar radiation, galactic cosmic rays, and micrometeorites have battered and weathered the surface. The material below should offer a better record of the moon’s origins, and JAXA aims to collect at least 10 grams of it.

MMX will carry both the Idefix rover [bottom] and a robotic coring sampler [top] designed to dig beneath Phobos’s weathered surface.JAXA

The pneumatic sampler takes a different approach. Mounted on one of the lander’s legs, it will inject pure, non-reactive nitrogen gas into the surface and capture the grains stirred up. This sample could illuminate the changes Mars and its moons have undergone over time. The dual system also adds redundancy in the face of Phobos’s unknowns. “If the surface of Phobos proves to be very hard, [the coring sampler] may struggle to penetrate the ground. [The pneumatic sampler] would not experience this issue and still be able to gather material,” Kawakatsu says.

One of the most intriguing aspects of MMX is the additional possibility of collecting material from the planet below. It’s likely that Phobos has been peppered by Martian ejecta thrown into space by meteor impacts, so MMX also provides an opportunity to return the first Martian samples to Earth. Michel estimates that the samples could contain “a few hundred grains coming from Mars.” Scientists can distinguish those grains from native Phobos material by analyzing their oxygen isotopes.

That possibility raises a planetary-protection question. A direct Mars sample-return mission would have to follow strict rules to ensure that potentially living biological material from Mars doesn’t contaminate Earth. But those protocols don’t apply to MMX, even if its sample does collect grains of Martian soil. A panel of experts concluded that any microbes blasted off Mars wouldn’t survive the violent impact and ejection or the intense radiation exposure on the way to Phobos. This saved MMX from implementing expensive and time-consuming quarantine and containment protocols for the returning sample.

After landing on Phobos, MMX will have roughly two hours to collect samples from the moon’s surface before lifting off again.JAXA

During the brief surface operation, the robotic arm will deposit the samples in a storage unit, from which they’ll be transferred into a capsule aboard the return module and sealed in a vacuum. After that, lift off.

Once back in Mars orbit, the exploration module will resume its observations of Phobos and make several flybys of Mars’s other diminutive moon, Deimos, to gather data on its surface, structure, and composition. In November 2030, during a favorable alignment of Mars and Earth, MMX will begin the homeward leg of its trip. The return module will separate from the exploration module and power the voyage home, its sole objective to bring the dust of Phobos to Earth.

MMX’s sample return capsule will carry material from Phobos through Earth’s atmosphere in 2031.JAXA

Finally, in 2031, the 60-centimeter-wide sample capsule will plunge into Earth’s atmosphere at roughly 12 kilometers per second. Assuming it survives the extreme heat of reentry and lands safely in Australia, scientists will begin to tease out clues about Phobos and the early solar system. JAXA’s Institute of Space and Astronautical Science will receive and curate the samples, which will also be shared with mission partners.

“We have macroscale measurements from the spacecraft, microscale measurements with the rover, and then sample analysis,” Michel says. “So we can relate the three kinds of scales together because we have all of them.” The insights gleaned from orbital images, close-up images of the regolith, and the chemical analysis of the samples could have wider implications for our understanding of our solar system.

“MMX is a mission to understand the Mars system and shed light onto how terrestrial planets like the Earth, and maybe Mars, develop a habitable environment,” Kawakatsu says. “We strongly suspect that our terrestrial planet region formed dry, and water and organics were scattered inwards from the icy-rich outer solar system.” Mars, he says, sits at the gateway between the inner and outer solar system, making its moons valuable witnesses to the processes that shaped potentially habitable worlds.

Andrew Jones is a freelance journalist based near Helsinki. He writes about the space industry and technology with a particular focus on China's activities.

The communications blackout offers a chance to learn things about handling errors autonomously and recording and storing data autonomously that should useful for other deep space missions. I wonder what the engineers are most worried about for that phase of the mission!

Apple has released iOS 27.3 public beta 2 for iPhone. Today’s release also includes a new build for iOS 27.3 beta 2 for developers. The update brings new Calendar controls, more Siri AI capabilities, and new features for iPhone Duo. It also includes the redesigned Health app and other changes introduced earlier this month.

The update follows yesterday’s second developer beta and the first public beta on November 5.

Apple has also detailed higher daily usage limits for Siri AI and other Apple Intelligence features through eligible iCloud+ plans. Plans with 200GB or more include extra capacity; the 50GB plan keeps standard limits.

See our full iOS 27.3 beta 2 roundup for more on the latest discoveries.

The first public beta brought back the redesigned Health app after its earlier preview during iOS 27.2 testing. On iPhones with Apple Intelligence support, Insights collects trends across your health data, while Longevity includes a Health Age comparison based on Apple Watch measurements.

If you’re already testing the public beta, open Settings > General > Software Update to check for the new version.

Joining for the first time? Make a backup, then enroll in the free Apple Beta Software Program using your iPhone’s Apple Account. In Settings > General > Software Update > Beta Updates, choose iOS 27 Public Beta. Go back to Software Update to download and install it.

‘They Will Kill You’ will have you thoroughly entertained (and speechless)

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

2026 has been a pretty decent year for new movies so far, but that doesn’t mean we’ve escaped the usual problem of some genuinely entertaining releases slipping under the radar. One such film is “They Will Kill You,” a gloriously bonkers mash-up of survival, comedy and horror that pits a tough-as-nails woman against a group of seriously unhinged cult members. The whole thing feels like a fever dream, with outrageous violence, ridiculous twists and enough carnage to keep you wondering what on earth you’re watching.

Thankfully, Prime Video has now added “They Will Kill You” to its library, which I’m hoping will give this overlooked gem a chance to find a much bigger audience. Its theatrical run certainly didn’t do it any favors, with the movie reportedly earning approximately $19 million worldwide against a production budget of $20 million, making it a box office disappointment. That’s a shame, because while it’s not a perfect film by any means, it’s certainly not a bad one.

In fact, I’d argue it’s one of the more entertaining horror releases of the year so far. It knows exactly how ridiculous it wants to be and has plenty of fun with its increasingly chaotic set pieces. I left the theater genuinely shocked by some of the things I witnessed, but also grinning at just how much fun I'd had. If you missed it on the big screen, its arrival on Prime Video is a pretty good excuse to put that right, and here’s why.

“They Will Kill You” follows Asia Reaves (Zazie Beetz), a young woman who takes a live-in housekeeping job at The Virgil, a luxurious New York City apartment building, hoping to find her missing younger sister, Maria (Myha'la). However, Asia soon discovers that the building’s wealthy residents are hiding a terrifying secret: they’re members of a satanic cult that has been sacrificing unsuspecting workers for decades.

When the residents attempt to make Asia their latest victim, they quickly discover she’s not quite as helpless as they expected. Trapped inside the building with seemingly no way out, Asia must fight her way through its corridors and take on an increasingly dangerous group of attackers. With time running out and Maria caught up in the cult’s plans, Asia faces a brutal fight to get them both out alive.

I’ll admit, I was a little worried “They Will Kill You” might struggle to stand out, especially arriving shortly after “Ready or Not 2,” which has a pretty similar premise involving two sisters trying to escape a cult. Thankfully, Zazie Beetz gives this film a flavor of its own. She’s an absolute badass, throwing herself into some wonderfully chaotic fight scenes and getting covered in blood more times than I can count. There’s also a noticeably angrier edge to this movie, which I really appreciated. It’s a welcome addition to the horror-comedy genre that isn’t afraid to get properly nasty.

Storytelling isn’t exactly the film’s strong suit, and I wouldn’t say it does anything particularly compelling with its characters or central plot. But that’s not really why I’d recommend it. The real draw is the action, inventive kill scenes and completely unhinged body horror. There are also some wonderfully ridiculous twists involving the cult that had me laughing, while the final act goes so completely off the rails that I was practically squealing (little hint there). It’s an absolute hoot, and I had a ridiculous amount of fun watching it.

Sign up to the weekly Tom's Streaming Guide to stay in the loop with the latest releases and top recommendations across your favorite streaming services. We’ve got you covered with a complete guide on what’s worth watching.

I also really enjoyed the film’s visual style. Director Kirill Sokolov uses graphic compositions that sometimes resemble comic-book panels, alongside unusual framing and some wonderfully eccentric camera angles. There are moments when the whole thing almost feels like you’re watching a video game, particularly during its more elaborate fight sequences. Yes, it’s a little unconventional, but I thought it worked brilliantly with the film’s exaggerated violence and chaotic energy. It gives “They Will Kill You” a distinct visual identity that helps it stand apart from other horror-comedies.

There’s definitely a lack of genuine character connection here, largely because the story doesn’t give you much to work with, but Beetz is such a compelling screen presence that you naturally find yourself rooting for her anyway. She’s more than capable of carrying the film, and I’d happily watch her take on another ridiculous survival scenario. I also think “They Will Kill You” has some serious cult classic potential. It might not have found its audience at the box office back in March, but I wouldn't be surprised if it earns a lot more love in the years ahead as more people discover it. Sometimes all a film needs is a second chance, and this one certainly deserves it.

Stream "They Will Kill You" on Prime Video now

Alix is a Senior Streaming Writer at Tom’s Guide, which basically means watching the best movies and TV shows and then writing about them. It’s a dream job for someone who’s been obsessed with storytelling since she first figured out how to work a remote.

Before joining Tom’s Guide, Alix honed her skills as a staff writer with outlets like Screen Rant and Bough Digital, where she discovered her love for the entertainment industry.

She heads to the cinema every week as a tradition, no matter what’s showing. For her, movies aren’t just entertainment — they’re a ritual, a comfort, and a constant source of inspiration. When she’s not at her desk or at the cinema, you’ll probably find her deep into a horror video game on her PC.

#3247. AI Agents Are Testing the Limits of Zero-Trust Security

As autonomous AI agents work together, verifying their actions, enforcing security policies, and maintaining accountability becomes increasingly difficult

Vishal Sharma is a Reader in the School of Electronics, Electrical Engineering, and Computer Science at Queen's University Belfast, Northern Ireland, United Kingdom.

In a de-authentication attack on an aerial vehicle using a human- and agent-in-the-loop approach, an AI agent can quickly scan the active channel and autonomously intercept traffic, thus reducing the time to react and regain control.

This article is brought to you by Queen’s University Belfast.

Several teams around the globe are leveraging AI by creating a task force of agents managed by an orchestrator and creating applications to support risk assessment, client profiling, match making, and information yield with a slight overview of decision making. One of the important components for these agents is to ensure that the logs are managed and historic relevance is not being used to avoid skewing towards same decision making. Thus, the system is expected to keep checkpoints in place where agents are prompted to delete such historic relevance.

However, despite such methodology in place, a future prompt could make the agents bring forward the information that was supposed to be deleted and can be tricked into revealing more information, which is a classic case of context recovery attack. So, the question raised here is: How can we trust that our instructions have been followed? And where is the proof?

There is an element of utilizing zero-trust architectures (ZTA) for orchestrating and managing agentic activity, which simply means all agentic interactions use the core principle of “never trust,” “always verify.” ZTA components include a policy enforcement point (PEP) that has to be trusted to maintain trust across the system, so the question that remains is where is the component of zero-trust, and shall we trust the policies enforced by PEP?

Having a pro-agentic approach and utilizing agents could be helpful with the right guardrails in place. Opening our systems to random agents that are being trained on off-the-shelf models and blindly relying on them can pose significant cyber risks. For example, vibe coding by using an AI model to help develop software, giving away the entire codebase to an untrusted entity outside the organization can lead to vulnerability sweeping across multiple surfaces.

Vibe coding by using an AI model to help develop software, giving away the entire codebase to an untrusted entity outside the organization can lead to vulnerability sweeping across multiple surfaces.

This opens critical discussions towards how vibe coding could interfere with the positioning and implementation of trusted execution of the agentic queries. Consider an autonomous web of agents that relies on agents’ inputs to drive the operations. When the system is operating under low tolerance of failure and with non-tracking based agentic workflows, it could be computationally expensive to trust and verify each query in real-time that leads to the common trade-offs of memory vs execution.

Another risk to consider is the zero-day attack. When it happens, how will the system react? Would such an event be manageable without a total infrastructure breakdown? The scale of impact can be observed from over reliance on agentic ecosystems with only one trusted layer. This could mean that when failure occurs, the entire ecosystem could be exposed, just like there will be no autonomy if the backbone network is not available, which essentially means no layer to place trust.

An in-house experiment done at Queen’s University Belfast (QUB) provided an initial understanding of how the scale of agentic attacks could mean a lower window of vulnerability. The team focused on very popular de-authentication attacks and with agentic orchestration, the swift rate to do de-authentication attacks could go as low as 2 to 3 seconds. This gives little to no time to react and decide on patching the system.

There is another aspect of the large-scale agentic system, which establishes trust under asynchronous autonomy. Trust serves as a critical foundation for traceability. How would you ensure that all the agents operating towards a common goal are aligned and understand the delays associated with their goals?

Our team worked around this space, which at first involved demonstrating that the problem exists, and its impact and scale can be huge when you must prove trust under boundaries of asynchronous autonomy. Solutions towards such problems can be simplified by keeping things like AI-bill of material or leveraging distributed ledger technology that can provide underlying infrastructure of trust via traceability and immutability and keep the agentic activity and associated trust vectors agnostic to the platform.

Within trust, another factor that is not well explored but needs a thorough investigation is the concept of horizontal anomalies. It defines how agents interact differently with various sources under different settings. As agents behave correctly and align themselves with the architectural expectations for one specific task or application, that does not necessarily mean these can be trusted for their operations across all associated components. How to identify such anomalies and what methods can be employed without complying with such agents remain open questions and topics for further exploration.

The critical aspect is that utility of agents with semi to low trust governance offer short-term high benefits, but the cost of recovery when the system fails is yet to be explored, and this will not be a contained issue. We are looking into the system where agents are already sweeping into different entities and may not allow complete recovery. For example, a mere supply chain issue because an agent going rogue is now not a containable small task but needs sweeping across all the touch points of those affected agents. This essentially means despite the number of agents and their ability to trigger proxy-agents, which may not be directly linked to the wider ecosystem, there is a need to ensure that computationally expensive trackers are in place for all the agents.

Other relevant PhD works carried out in our research group are towards sovereignty of AI, exploring aspects of trust and accountability. Our hypothesis is that sovereignty and trust need to be governed together as onus of provenance is high on the host of agents. Thus, it needs understanding of laws governing trust-based executions of AI. The important challenge here is that there is a vital difference between missed information and missed instructions, and both have different impacts when it comes to trusted accountability.

The real-world issue with these systems lies in the failure to adopt approaches that historically have relied on state-based modeling when governing trust. In stateless systems where agentic autonomy is high, the convergence and reliability towards trust-provenance decreases significantly. Thus, it brings us back to the original question – does a true zero-trust even exist?

Can policies be trusted? If so, how should these be managed without falling into the trap of policy-based accessibility and control issues? Despite the argument that PEP can help manage access between the agents, placing a single entity and expecting it to scale towards all agentic interactions is underestimating the problem space.

Formal verification of trust is another part of a trust-based agentic ecosystem. When dealing with AI models, understanding the robustness helps to put trust in place for these models.

To build our case and settle around the challenges of trust embeddings in Agentic AI, within Cyber AI hub, we are exploring opportunities to help companies scale up as well as build their pipeline of agentic applications for commercial viability. However, the element that governs our regular work and decision making are scale of problem and number of agentic deployments, anomaly detection across the agentic workflows, continuous evaluation of the attack surfaces and vulnerability assessment, exploring differences in the pure agentic AI and task-driven multi-agent system.

We are working with industries where trust is a pre-requisite, and these organizations put trust as a guardrail managed via internal policies with a pure focus on securing the systems through policies rather than trusting the third-party agentic service providers. Additionally, trust in services is presented by ensuring constraints around their service models where agentic activities are tracked and managed via logs including management of their token revocation list to avoid replay attacks depending on the type of application. Formal verification of trust is another part of a trust-based agentic ecosystem. When dealing with AI models, understanding the robustness helps to put trust in place for these models. Things like balancing the adversarial accuracy along with certified adversarial robustness can help to determine how much the model can be trusted.

But the question is, can we settle for anything less than foolproof when it comes to deployment of agents in the real world? And if so, how much impact can be controlled, and who is responsible for the remaining component?

If you’re looking for a gift for a DIY enthusiast in your life, or if you have some big home projects to tackle over the winter, you might be looking for some new tools. If you’re looking to save money, Black Friday sales are often the lowest prices of the year on quality tools. Here are some of the best early Black Friday 2026 tool deals you can snag right now at Lowe’s.

Cordless power tools are a game changer for DIY projects and home maintenance because they’re compact and portable and they allow you to drive screws and bolts, drill holes, and make cuts for tasks like patching drywall, putting up shelves, or adding hardware to cabinets. Saving some money on good quality cordless tools can help you save on replacing your tools and batteries down the road too.

The DeWalt 20-volt MAX cordless drill is on sale for $99, 44% off its regular price. This tool comes with a 20-volt, 2-amp-hour battery and a charger. This is the first tool I would buy if I were starting a new tool set because it allows you to drive screws as well as drill holes.

The DeWalt 20-volt MAX cordless oscillating multi-tool kit is on sale for $99, 50% off its usual price. This set comes with a 2-amp-hour battery, a charger, three starter blades, four pieces of sandpaper, a sanding attachment, and a depth guide. This tool is very handy for a home tool set because you can use it to plunge-cut drywall, trim wooden moulding, cut PVC pipe, and shape tile.

The DeWalt 20-volt MAX 4.5” paddle switch angle grinder is on sale for $209, 47% off its typical price. This tool comes with a 2-amp-hour battery and a 4-amp-hour battery. You’ll need a 20-volt DeWalt charger to use it. This is a good tool for metalworking and for trimming the ends of nails and screws that poke through.

Having the right hand tools is crucial for successful DIY projects, and having the right bits and accessories saves a lot of time lost to taking extra trips to the hardware store while you’re working.

The Craftsman 242-piece mechanics tool set is on sale for $99, 56% off its regular price. The set comes with a ¼-inch, a ⅜-inch, and a ½-inch drive ratchet, sockets in standard and metric sizes, a set of box wrenches, a set of driver bits, a driver handle, a set of Allen keys, and a toolbox. This is a good set to start a hand tool collection with, especially for working on vehicles or home maintenance projects like changing air filters.

The DeWalt 110-piece bit set is on sale for $29.98, 40% off its usual price. The set comes with a set of multimaterial drill bits, a set of extended shaft driver bits, a magnetic bit sheath, and several types of standard driver tips. This is a good set for most DIY projects.

The DeWalt 35-piece driver bit set is on sale for $9.98, 41% off its typical price. This set comes with driver tips in a variety of standard types and a bit sheath for driving longer screws. This is a good basic set that can be used with your driver to assemble flat-pack furniture, swap hardware on drawers and cabinets, or tighten squeaky door hinges.

The best early deals on tools right now are at Home Depot, where you can get up to 65% off on select Milwaukee tools, 50% off on DeWalt tools, and 30% off on Ryobi tools. They also have several offers for over 50% off on hand tools.

Home Depot and Lowe’s often compete with each other for seasonal sales, so it’s always a good idea to check both sites before buying. Right now, Home Depot has the best deals on DeWalt and Milwaukee cordless tool sets, but Lowe’s has a better deal on Craftsman hand tool sets.

The best prices of the year on tools are during the holidays in November and December. This is because of the holiday shopping push, as well as making space for new tools that come out in the spring. The second-best time to buy tools is in May and June during Father’s Day sales.

#3244. ‘The Gilded Age’ Star Morgan Spector Breaks Down “Exactly The Wrong Time” For George’s [Spoiler] & “Parallels” Between Anti-Monopoly Legislation And ParaBros Merger In Season 4

SPOILER ALERT: This post contains spoilers for The Gilded Age Season 4’s fourth episode.

George Russell’s gunshot wound is coming back to haunt him in a way as Season 4 of The Gilded Age reaches its midpoint.

As has been building since last season when George survived an assassination attempt in his home, a troubling laudanum addiction has come to light for the railroad tycoon, whose behavior early on in the season has grown more and more unpredictable.

“I think it is fairly easy, when you have a long-term injury, and you do have lingering pain, to fall into opiate addiction. I think that is a real thing, but I also think George is someone with a really indomitable will. And I think for someone like him, in our story, to slip into the situation, I think there’s something else going on in his life,” Spector told Deadline. “I think that something else is the destabilization of his relationship with Bertha. I don’t think that’s entirely it. I think, after the shooting last season, he’s really having a gigantic midlife crisis. He’s built this enormous empire, and he’s suddenly realized he doesn’t really know who he is anymore, what his values are, and if and if he wants to keep living his life the way he has been, so I think the laudanum comes along at just exactly the wrong time for him.”

George is under extra pressure this season with President Grover Cleveland (Jim Gaffigan) in town and working on antitrust legislature, which would threaten the railroad monopoly he has worked so hard to construct and protect. Add J.D. Rockefeller (Neal Huff) into the equation wanting to cut back prices he pays Russell Industries to transport his oil, and George feels very cornered in business. Spector had hinted that his character was already having a “crisis of conflict” in Season 3. Watch on Deadline

“Rockefeller was this really interesting character, and so we learned more about him from the research. I’m from Cleveland, and he’s originally from Cleveland. And he basically bankrupted Toledo or some city. He ripped them off, but he was also really pious, and he did do the price fixing,” co-showrunner Sonja Warfield told Deadline. “That’s something he did do. He was ruthless in business, but in church all the time. I love to put characters under pressure. I think it’s where the magic happens, and George and the laudanum —Doctor [Erica] Dunbar had actually suggested that last season.”

The tincture of opium was prescribed by the white doctor who attended to George’s gunshot wound after Dr. William Kirkland (Jordan Donica) saved Mr. Russell’s life in Season 3.

“She did say, ‘You know that you can get addicted to it,’ and so we planted that last season, and what I love is that, Morgan plays it just so deftly and just beautifully — this vulnerable side of George. And in the first season we see George, there’s a character who gets down on his knees and begs him, ‘Spare us,’ and now George is is really at his knees [on this],” Warfield said.

RELATED: RELATED: ‘The Gilded Age’ Producers Address George’s Shocking Decision In Season 3 Finale: “He Feels Bertha Made Him Act Against His Instincts”

Will Morris (Will Pullen) turned out to be the man responsible for the attempt on George’s life, and there is history between the two, because Will is the son of Patrick Morris, the business partner of George’s who took his own life in Season 1 after a deal he made with railroad magnate went bad.

A meeting with Daniel Manning, Secretary of the Treasury during the first two years of Grover Cleveland’s presidency is one of the last instinces of Season 4 in which George exhibits normal behavior despite his substance abuse. It’s explicitly established during that chat that President Cleveland thinks “monopolies threaten our way of government.” George wants to meet with the president, and also Rockefeller, to convince the United States leader that he could gain him political backing in New York for re-election, which George things is iffy for Cleveland. Vieweres can’t help but notice similarities with the merger taking place between Paramount and Warner Bros.

“About the merger thing, Julian and Sonia have a really fantastic record of being a little clairvoyant in terms of the things that they choose to take on in these seasons, and I think partly that’s because there are just so many structural parallels between the era at the end of the 19th century and the era we’re living in now in terms of wealth inequality and concentration of monopoly power,” Spector said. “And what’s fascinating is that those structural similarities create really similar consequences, and that’s because of the way capitalism works. These are systemic dynamics, and they play out in similar ways, no matter what time you’re living in. So yeah, I think either Julian is Nostradamus or maybe there are some structural issues with our political economic system.”

George also confronts Rockefeller at the gentleman’s club they both frequent for business and social life, displaying increasingly erratic behavior and raised voice, as he communicates to the oil baron his plan to get President Cleveland on their side.

A physical therapist explains when to start prehab and shares four moves to build strength before surgery

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

If you’re scheduled for an upcoming hip or knee replacement surgery, you’re far from alone. The American Joint Replacement Registry, managed by the American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, has surpassed 4.3 million hip and knee replacement procedures in its database. People heading into these operations have often spent months or years modifying how they move because of hip or knee pain, which can leave the muscles around the joints weaker than they should be.

The good news? Prehab—a structured strengthening program you do before surgery—can help strengthen your knee and hip joints. A 2026 systematic review found early benefits for pain management, mobility, and functionality in people who underwent knee replacement surgery.

“Surgery addresses the damaged joint, but patients still need strength to regain mobility and participate in rehabilitation afterward,” says Kaylee LeCavalier, PT, DPT, SCS, CSCS, CAPS, a physical therapist and board-certified sports specialist.

Here’s how early to start prehab, how often to do it, and the four moves that LeCavalier recommends before surgery.

“Building strength takes time, and starting earlier provides more opportunity to progressively increase resistance and improve physical capacity before surgery,” explains LeCavalier. “Research suggests benefits in programs lasting 6 to 8 weeks, but no optimal duration has been established.”

If your surgery is closer than that, don’t dismiss the benefits of doing prehab. “Even with only a few weeks available, patients can still make meaningful progress toward preparing their bodies for surgery and recovery,” LeCavalier says.

For most people, LeCavalier recommends doing strength training two to three days per week, and allowing for proper recovery between more intense sessions. However, how often you should train depends on your beginning strength, activity level, pain, and how well you tolerate the exercises.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

LeCavalier recommends starting each session with a short warm-up, such as a few minutes of walking or stationary cycling, then move into the strengthening work with enough rest between sets to ensure you’re using proper technique. She stresses that “exercises need to provide enough resistance to challenge the muscles.”

Bodyweight exercises are an excellent starting point if you have significant pain or limited strength in your knees or hips. As the moves get easier, you can add weights, use stronger resistance bands or progress to harder variations. A good sign that you’re ready to progress is when you can consistently complete the sets and reps with proper form and control and without a significant increase in pain or swelling during exercise or the following day.

The leg press helps strengthen the major muscles around your hips and knees and is one of the few exercises with research behind it before knee replacement.

Both of these moves help build the strength you need to get up from a seated position and support your body weight during daily activities. Sit-to-stands are often a more beginner-friendly exercise, while squats are a foundational compound exercise that you can progress toward.

Your hip abductors help stabilize your pelvis when you stand on one leg, which is essential for walking and climbing stairs.

Step-ups focus on one leg at a time, which can help improve mobility and strength in your hips and knees.

Electronic products now pack circuits, structures, thermal paths, and packaging into very small spaces. These physical domains interact with one another. A packaging choice can change how a shock load reaches a circuit board. Such interactions are hard to predict. Most are found during physical qualification, late in development. At that stage, the design is mostly fixed. A failure leads to redesign, rebuilds, and retesting. Physical tests give strong evidence of robustness, but they give limited insight into load paths and failure margins. Traditional simulation gives more detail, but it needs specialist skills and long manual setup. This white paper explains how guided virtual validation brings shock and drop assessment into the design phase. It reviews common test configurations, model inputs, and acceptance criteria. A packaged drop case study then shows how packaging can be optimized across all drop orientations and checked against physical test results.

#3241. This Note-Taking Pebble Ring Is so Simple, and I Love It

Pebble’s $75 ring, the Index 01, has one job: It lets you record voice memos. That seems like it would be underwhelming, and the idea was ridiculed by some of Pebble’s fans when the product was first announced. But I’ve been wearing it for a few weeks, and folks: I love it.

In this era where every tech product is trying to also be every other tech product, I appreciate the Index’s simplicity. This is a ring with no heart rate sensors or even charging pins, just a microphone, a button to activate it, and a light to let you know that it’s working. The audio is processed on your device; no need to send anything to the cloud.

To buy the Index 01 ring, you get yourself a sizing kit (either buy one for $10 or 3D print it yourself), order the ring, and pair it with the Pebble app on your phone. I use an iPhone rather than an Android, which means I can’t use certain features like setting timed reminders or connecting to Beeper, but it’s still an incredibly useful little device. The Index has no charger, since it uses a disposable battery that Pebble estimates will last about two years.

The simplest way to use the Index is to wear it on your index finger (hence the name, get it?) and press the button with your thumb. Speak a quick note while holding the button in, and the ring will flash to let you know it got the message. A moment later, you’ll get a notification saying that it added (whatever you said) to your “Notes to self” note.

To take this further, you can create different notes and ask the ring to add what you say to a specific note. You can also double-click the button to ask a question. The answer will appear in the notification you get on your phone or watch a moment later. (The ring does not speak to you.)

All the notes you leave yourself appear as plain text in the Pebble app, fully editable. If you tap on each one, you can see a timestamp from when you left the note, and you can replay the voice recording if the transcription doesn’t make sense. (Why is there a “pencil sharp pepper” on my packing list? Ohh, that’s a pencil sharpener.) You can also add notes by typing them, which I find useful when starting a to-do list or a packing list.

It’s incredible how useful a simple timestamped note can be. I used to do something similar with my “notes to self” chat in Signal, but the Index makes it even easier since I won’t get distracted by opening my phone. For example, I make a note on the Index whenever I take a medication, so that tomorrow morning I will be able to check whether I already took, say, a long-acting allergy pill. (You do not want to accidentally double up on those.)

There’s one thing that, for years, I wished for a simple tool to help me do. It’s trivial, which makes it extra frustrating that I have not been able to find a good solution. I would simply like to note when I leave for a road trip, and when I start and end each stop. This way I can tell how long the driving took as a portion of the whole trip, and how long my stops tend to be so I can plan them better next time.

You’d think this would be easy, but every existing tool drove me nuts in a different way. Stopwatches only store a single number, so I can’t break down how long each stop was—and if I miss a button press, I’m screwed. Sending myself a Signal text is probably my best option, but if I’ve just parked my car after three hours of driving, the second I pick up my phone I’m going to see all the notifications that arrived while I was on the road, and I’ll forget to actually send that text.

But this is exactly what the Index does well. I don’t even need to open my phone or look at my watch. Pressing the button with my thumb means I can do this one-handed without having a microphone always listening. (It’s also a great way to jot down the random things I think of while driving.)

The Index worked perfectly for my travel log, and I even used it for a workout after I got to my hotel room that night. I’d do 10 pushups, then tell the ring “add 10 pushups to my workout.” I’d do 20 crunches, and add that as well. I left the workout note open on my phone and could glance over and see what I had already done, since my messages got added to the note as I went.

I didn’t need a workout app for any of this, or a special-purpose travel app. I can just leave myself a dang note, and the note-taking app can remember when I left the note and, if I choose, play back exactly how I said it. It’s gloriously simple. Good job, Pebble.

#3238. ‘The Gilded Age’ Star Denée Benton Talks Peggy’s “Victory Lap” & “Ambitious Tension” In Her Marriage To Dr. Kirkland

SPOILER ALERT: This post contains spoilers for The Gilded Age Season 4’s fourth episode.

As if a new house and husband weren’t enough, Peggy Scott (Denée Benton), now Mrs. Dr. William Kirkland, receives a letter from journalist Ida B. Wells about her newly published book in the fourth episode of Season 4 of The Gilded Age.

The recognition for her novel could be seen as the cherry on top of a wonderful new chapter for the journalist, writer and now wife, whose wedding unfolded in episode 403.

“It’s really fun to see Peggy step into her Renaissance woman era. She’s striving so much for the first few seasons. It’s very ‘Don’t believe me? Just watch’ like everything that she’s getting to do in Season 4,” Benton told Deadline. “Since Season 1, she’s like, ‘I told y’all, you didn’t believe me, but it’s okay.’ And now it’s nice to see her do her victory lap.” Watch on Deadline

Peggy is now part of a union, though, and while her star is on the rise, her husband isn’t currently satisfied at his job. An old colleague of his, Dr. Harris (Dennis Haysbert) pinpoints this with William and suggests he look out for an opening back at Friedman’s Hospital, where Dr. Harris practices in Washington D.C. After discussing it with William, Dr. Harris brings it up with Peggy and both sets of parents of the newlyweds present, where he unintentionally causes some ripples.

“It’s also really nice to play with the ambitious tension that I recognize in Bertha, where there [are] these blinders on, and I was really thankful for how radical it was to see her completely lose sight for a time that she was in a pair and in a family,” Benton added. “It’s fun that the audience won’t always agree with [Peggy]. I think it adds a lot of dynamic texture to her not just having to be this moral gold star for the show, which is very limiting, but to have her lose sight of the fact that William is facing his own challenges, like the limitations of racism, not being able to practice surgery in New York and having a patient die because the white doctor didn’t tend to him. It’s not just as limited as a man having trouble with her ambitions. It’s ‘How do they really balance both of their dreams?’”

A very representative moment of such “ambitious tension’ between husband and wife arrives when one of Peggy’s colleagues, Mr. Simms, mistakenly calls her husband Mr. Scott instead of Dr. Kirkland at a reading and signing for her book. This scene stemmed from a real-life incident co-showrunner Sonja Warfield experienced at a writing event.

“I wasn’t even that much of an established writer, but I have always used my maiden name, even when I was married, and he got referred to as Mr. Warfield. And so I thought, what if that happened in 1885? What’s the impact of that? Especially if the parents are around to witness that, and what does that do to your masculinity then?” Warfield told Deadline. “Because men felt, probably, still to an extent, proprietary over their wives, right? Women really were barely dealing with their career versus family back then, and women worked, and a lot of Black women worked or expected to work and had to work.”

During a carriage ride home after the book signing, Dr. Kirkland tries to address the idea of moving to Washington D.C. with Peggy, who holds firm and wonders why they have to uproot at that exact moment. She doubles back and gives William recognition for his work, but she isn’t quite sold on them moving yet.

“Marriage is really about coming together and becoming one, and Peggy has lived a long time as an individual, and she was an only child, and so she got to do what she wanted,” Warfield said. “So, again, like with Enid and Oscar, marriage will be an eye opener for Peggy and William as well about gender roles, to an extent, because he’s the man, and so he’s supposed to have the last word about their lives, and that was what was expected back then. She would have no say.”

Peggy does holds her own when the discussion of children comes up — as it has now multiple times this season before and after she got married via her husband or his mother when she refers to grandchildren. This is, in addition to the lavender marriage aspect of Enid (Kelly Curran) and Oscar’s (Blake Ritson) union, what sets the women on different paths, since Enid keeps poking at the idea of having a child with Oscar, especially after Agnes van Rhijn (Christine Baranski) says she sees a glow about Enid signalling she could be with child in this latest episode.

“It’s cool to watch this power couple trailblaze and navigate what power looked like for them and her. Even seeing a woman at that time decide when or if she wants children, even now there’s still a little taboo for those of us who will admit out loud that we are not sure,” Benton said. “And so for a woman at that time to say, “We’ll see,” is wild, and then it’s really cool to see the ways Mrs. Kirkland is kind of right, where she’s like, ‘Listen, Peggy’s a great woman, but is she going to be a great wife to you?’ And what it means to run a household at that time is basically a full time job. lIt’s cool ike that [Peggy’s] getting to represent so many textures of womanhood and femininity.”

Warfield agreed with Benton’s assessment of the character.

“I think Peggy’s character does surprise us, as Denee said in her reaction to things. I think people think will think a lot of things,” the co-showrunner said. “People might get a little bit upset because Dr. Kirkland is a catch, and I’m sure there are going to be women out there who are saying, ‘Girl, if you don’t want him, then… [I’ll take him!]’”

#3237. Gemini Notebook's New Interactive Site Builder Is Much More Useful Than I Expected

David Nield is a technology journalist from Manchester in the U.K. who has been writing about gadgets and apps for more than 20 years.

He has a bachelor's degree in English Literature from Durham University, where he also spent a term as editor of the award-winning student newspaper Palatinate. His journalism career started in print media, where he contributed to and edited several technology magazines and bookazines sold in the U.K. and internationally. More recently, he has worked as a freelancer for some of the biggest technology publications on the web, covering everything from on-the-ground reporting about product launches, to detailed explainers and how-to guides on apps, gadgets, and platforms. His expertise covers broad areas of consumer tech, including smartphones, laptops, wearables, and AI.

Gemini Notebook, Google's AI tool for study and research, already lets you do a lot with your notes: You can turn them into flashcard quizzes, interactive podcasts, video explainers, mind maps, and infographics, as well as interrogating the sources you've collected through AI-powered prompts and responses. Now there's something new. You can also build interactive websites from your notebooks.

That might not immediately seem like the most obvious fit, turning your research notes into a mass of HTML code. But it gives you another way to look at your material and to get insights from it. Here's how it works, what you could potentially do with it, and how impressively it worked when I put it to the test on some early 20th-century Irish literature.

Website building is rolling out now for Gemini Notebook's web app for all users, and is "coming soon" to the mobile app.  You won't see a website option in the Studio panel alongside Audio Overview, Reports, Quiz, and the rest; instead, you type something along the lines of "make me a website" in the prompt box.

To make a website, you need sources, so I set Gemini Notebook to collect information about James Joyce's 1914 collection of short stories, Dubliners. As I studied Dubliners many years ago (I highly recommend it), I was hoping I'd spot any AI errors and hallucinations, and be able to properly assess the quality of Gemini Notebook's analysis.

With a suitable amount of information absorbed into the AI brain, I got Gemini Notebook to make me a website. Google doesn't give too much official guidance here, but says you should add "a description of what you want to build for work or study," so if you have a particular style or angle in mind, include it.

Here was my prompt: "Build a website using all the sources and information collected so far. Make it an interactive guide to the individual stories in Dubliners, as well as the overarching themes and context. I want to use it as a study aid to explore different aspects of the story collection."

The finished website pops up in the Studio panel, and in my case it took around five minutes to put something together from 26 different sources. Click on the website, and it opens in a new window—you can use it from there, open it in a separate tab, or download the code to your computer.

I was honestly impressed by how much Gemini Notebook managed to pack into a single website: I got plot summaries, analysis, critical context, and some of the main themes and motifs outlined. There was an interactive quiz at the bottom of the page to test my knowledge, and even a graphic I could click through to reveal different elements of how the stories fit together.

Everything was well laid out and functional, albeit with the standard "sheen" you get from anything made by AI (which tends to always pick the same colors and fonts). I wouldn't have necessarily thought that I needed a website if I was still studying Dubliners today, but I can definitely see how it would have helped.

For something like my project, a website really works well as a study aid, since it offers a different way of interrogating the information. You can already do that in the main chat, and with tools such as the audio and video overviews, but this is different. It's a bit like having a mini-Wikipedia focused just on whatever you're researching.

The interactive elements that are included—so in my example, I could click from story to story, and theme to theme, within the same page—make a site more engaging than a standard report document and a static wall of text, and should help the information stick if you're trying to study it.

I can also see how this might be useful for sharing data with others. Maybe you need to analyze monthly report figures, or you want to chart how your organization has developed a product over time—perhaps an interactive website will relay that information in a more compelling way than a slide deck or PDF.

Maybe you have a notebook stuffed with details of a big family vacation. Putting together a website through Gemini Notebook would give your family a hub that they could use to easily check up on the details of the trip—where you're going and when, what you'll see there, what they need to pack, and so on. Another idea might be a family tree, if you have ancestry data and sources packed together in a notebook. Putting together a website would be a great way to visualize it, and, again, it's something you could share with relatives. If there were updates to the data you've collected, you could generate a new website.

Bear in mind that you can do a lot with your prompt. My website turned out the way it did because that's what I asked for, and if you need more interactivity or specific types of sections, then you can ask. Based on my follow-up prompts, you can also specify colors and certain layout choices, though it's not quite a full-scale website builder.

It looks like these sites are single-page creations, though they do have interactive elements and sections that change as you click around. It might be better to think of them as mini apps rather than sites. As of yet, there's no built-in option for publishing a site online or sharing it with others, so you need to download the HTML and do that manually.

#3234. 10 Shows Like 'The Body' You Should Watch Next

Ross Johnson writes about television, film, and literature for Lifehacker. Entertainment.Ross produces the Swan Songs film podcast and hosts The Sound of Tomorrow, a pop culture and current affairs radio show based in Rochester, New York, where he lives with his husband and dogs and supports the local arts and cinema scene. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

Netflix's newest streaming hit, The Body, is drawing in millions of viewers, great reviews, and a gaggle of protests from people who didn't much care for the trailer. But if your lesbian-forward supernatural horror series isn't drawing cries of "blasphemy!"...what are you even doing? In that spirit, we'll conjure up some other shows dealing with the (extremely) dark side of high school.

This time-hopping survival drama is about a group of teenage girls who are stranded in the wilderness in 1996 and do terrible things to survive—the extent of which we only learn about via flashbacks from the present day, where the events of 19 months spent in the wild continue to resonate. There are ambiguous teases of the supernatural here (much more ambiguous than in The Body), but there's plenty of human-level horror as well. The show explores the nasty things we get up to when in survival mode (whether trapped in the wilds, stuck with other teenagers—or god forbid both at once), while also cynically (but accurately) positing that there's a huge difference between the version of the past we talk about and the one that really happened. Stream Yellowjackets on Paramount+.

Situated between flashbacks and flash-forwards (not entirely unlike Yellowjackets), mystery/thriller The Wilds sees an airplane full of teenage girls crash on the way to an empowerment program in Hawaii. It quickly becomes clear that the accident was engineered and that the whole thing is some sort of social experiment, and the survivors are forced to compete against each other if they want to live. The show understands the ways in which young women are exploited and expected to compete against each other in the real world, and the ways in which we'll do just about anything when survival is on the line. Stream The Wilds on Prime Video.

When pretty, popular girl Kate Wallis (Olivia Holt) goes missing without a trace in 1993, awkward Jeanette Turner (Chiara Aurelia) steps in to fill the gap, modeling herself after Kate by working her way into the missing girl's social circle and getting close with her boyfriend. That's all going great until Kate reappears two years later, accusing Jeanette of having witnessed the events around her disappearance and keeping quiet. Whoops. There's even more going on, as the show shifts back and forth between 1993, 1994, and 1995 to slowly reveal the missing pieces. Season two takes on a different story set in 1999 and 2000, and the forthcoming (surprise) third season will shake things up again. The emphasis here is on mystery, but it's a show about the aftereffects of trauma and of the dark secrets that can tear families and communities apart. Stream Cruel Summer on Hulu.

Juicy import Elite follows a group of working-class friends who earn scholarships to Las Encinas, a fictional private school that is, in the show’s universe, the most exclusive in Spain. What they find there is snobbery, mystery, murder, and lots and lots of sex (between and among characters of various sexual orientations and numerical groupings). The smart, wonderfully trashy show ran for a shocking (in our modern streaming era) eight seasons, with a couple of regional remakes. There's no supernatural stuff here, but plenty of dark deeds done with youthful vigor. Stream Elite on Netflix.

A teenager, Mae (Madeleine Arthur), is discovered by the side of the road with weird religious symbols carved into her skin. The hospital psychiatrist who treats her (Emily Deschanel) takes pity on, and interest in, Mae, deciding to take her in while arrangements can be made for a more permanent home for the cult escapee. Mae is, after all, level-headed and quiet, and couldn't possibly be any trouble. Hoo boy, yeah, that turns out to be a bad call on the good doctor's part. Stream Devil in Ohio on Netflix.

A different type of blasphemy at play here, in that Joan Lindsay's novel was already adapted brilliantly by Peter Weir in 1975, in a film often referred to as the greatest to come out of Australia. And yet, this Natalie Dormer-lead take is an achievement in its own right, the extended running time of a miniseries offering up more time to sit with the story's deliberately ineffable mysteries. Dormer plays Hester Appleyard, headmistress of a school for young ladies in the Australian bush. It's going well until a Valentine's Day picnic to the title's Hanging Rock sees three students and a governess disappear, impossibly, without a trace, bringing about the slow unravelling of pretty much everyone left behind. Stream Picnic at Hanging Rock on Prime Video and Tubi.

Mariam (Andria Tayeh) is brutally bullied by the cool clique at her private school in this Jordanian import, a high school drama that's both universal and distinctly Muslim in character. Fed up, Mariam convinces a couple of similarly outcast friends to join forces with her in a revenge plot that quickly gets out of hand. The show deals with Jordanian-style patriarchy head-on, without drawing any easy conclusions about its characters—Mariam catfishes one of her bullies and convinces her to send a revealing picture, one that she immediately posts, exploiting the very same repressive cultural elements that she claims to deplore. It's a smart, realist drama with soapy elements and nothing by way of the supernatural, but it's still a very sharp picture of the extremely cutthroat nature of high school life. Stream AlRawabi School for Girls on Netflix.

Peyton List stars as Maddie, a teenager in small-town Wisconsin for whom her death is very much just the beginning. Stuck in a high school in the afterlife (because hell is definitely for children), she goes on a journey to solve her own murder while uncovering secrets and lies in both worlds. It all sounds a bit grim, but the show has a sense of fun about it: While Maddie does develop the ability to communicate with the living, her world is populated by ghost teens from various eras and generations, with customs, mores, and cliques having developed in ghost high school just as in our world. Stream School Spirits on Paramount+.

The new Girigo app, claiming to grant wishes, sounds like harmless fun. Except, of course, that the things that teenagers want aren't always beneficent, and the app has already been the conduit for some incredibly dark deeds by the time it gets into the hands of the five high schoolers who find themselves caught in a Ring-like web of shamanistic horror and death countdowns. This is why we tell you to put your phones down once in a while... Stream If Wishes Could Kill on Netflix.

Four one-time best friends reunite at Rosewood High School a year after the disappearance of the leader of their little clique, all having received threatening messages from the mysterious "A," who knows everything they did last summer...and pretty much all the rest of the time. Shoplifting, parents having affairs, students hooking up with teachers—you name it, it's happening in town, and A knows it all. After the prime suspect turns up dead, the girls are caught in the killer's web while trying to keep their secrets hidden. If seven juicy seasons and three A's aren't enough for you, there are three spin-offs. Stream Pretty Little Liars on Hulu and HBO Max.
